10751-oregon-washington-and-alaska-sight:
E. L. Lomax, general passenger agent of the Union Pacific System, issued Oregon, Washington and Alaska: Sights and Scenes for the Tourist in 1890. The guide, offered by the railway's passenger department at Omaha, lists agents from Albany to Boston and points travelers toward the Pacific Northwest and Alaska. Illustrations show the lands the trains served.

The book mixes practical travel help with praise for scenery, towns, and routes. It captures the booster spirit of western railways, eager to fill their cars with tourists. Modern readers get a period guide to the Northwest, and a record of how railroads sold the West.
10958-an-unwilling-maid-being-the-histor:
Jeanie Gould Lincoln set this 1897 romance in Connecticut and New York during the American Revolution. Betty Yorke, born Wolcott, is a spirited young woman whose loyalties are tested by war, family, and love. Chapters follow her through bullets for defence, a prisoner named Oliver, a journey inside British lines, and the De Lancey ball, where love and loyalty pull opposite ways.

Betty's maid Moppet, a knot of rose-coloured ribbon, and a face on the wall add mystery and humour to the plot. Lincoln writes for young readers, keeping the history light but present: Whigs and Tories, couriers, and divided towns. The novel charms through Betty herself, unwilling at first, brave when it counts, and loyal to her own heart.
12667-travels-of-richard-and-john-lander:
Robert Huish compiled this 1836 account from the papers of Richard and John Lander, who sought the course and end of the River Niger. It opens with a survey of earlier African travellers, including Park, Denham, and Clapperton, before following the Landers inland. Markets, rulers, deserts, and river towns fill the long road south.

The narrative stresses hardship as much as discovery: heat, hunger, hostile bands, and long waits for guides and safe passage. Huish frames the journey as a key step in mapping West Africa for British readers. The book remains a full, first-hand record of exploration before steam and rail changed the continent.
1310-the-annals-of-the-parish-or-the-chr:
John Galt tells, year by year, the chronicle of Dalmailing, a Scottish parish, through the voice of its minister, Micah Balwhidder. From 1760 to 1809 the parish changes: mills rise, roads come, wars take sons, and old customs fade, all noted with a minister's dry humor.

Galt writes Scots life with warmth and realism, and the annals form a social history in miniature. The book made his name and founded the Scottish parish tale. It suits readers who like quiet chronicles and the texture of a community changing. Galt's parish chronicle gives a whole community's change in miniature.
13183-in-the-days-of-chivalry-a-tale-of-:
Evelyn Everett-Green's tale of the Black Prince's time opens in the warm autumn of Gascony, where forests turn russet, scarlet, and gold. Twin eaglets are the book's young heroes. They grow up among knights, priests, and woodmen. Chapters run from Father Anselm to the King, the Prince, and the war path. Everett-Green writes for young readers who love romance and history.

Later pages debate free will, with one speaker denying that God binds men's wills or makes them blind agents. An old man steeped in Moorish lore is blamed for gaining mastery over minds, not by demons but by wicked will. Joan Vavasour, kind and firm, promises care for an old servant's wife. The tale mixes chivalry, faith, and adventure in the old style.
13485-an-enquiry-concerning-the-principl:
Frances Reynolds asks in 1785 where our ideas of beauty come from, and what taste, grace, and genius share. Her enquiry, reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society with an introduction by James L. Clifford, argues that grace in the object, genius in making it, and taste in perceiving it are one quality seen from three sides.

Grace, she says, rests more on mental than bodily beauty, and sits between sublimity, which no rules can teach, and lower pleasures. Flowers please, she suggests, when they resemble a pre-formed idea of beauty in the human species, even when the mind cannot name the cause. Reynolds writes as a woman thinker of her age, plain, careful, and eager to ground feeling in reason.
13531-amos-kilbright-his-adscititious-ex:
Frank R. Stockton's 1888 collection opens with Amos Kilbright and his adscititious experiences, told by Richard Colesworthy, a practical attorney in an eastern town. Colesworthy, little given to speculative theory outside his profession, lends weight to a strange tale of a man acted upon by unseen powers.

Other stories follow: The Reversible Landscape, Dusky Philosophy in two expositions, and Plain Fishing. One exposition tells of seven devils, with Brother Peter closing his Bible with a bang though he cannot read a word of it. He preaches that women, possessed sevenfold, should submit to male direction. Stockton mixes fantasy, satire, and dry American humour throughout.
13887-dr-allinson-s-cookery-book-compris:
T. R. Allinson published Dr. Allinson's Cookery Book in 1915 as a guide to vegetarian cooking. A long index lists dishes from almond cheesecakes and apple charlotte to orange mould and pancake pudding. A month's menu for one person helps beginners plan meals. Allinson, a doctor, links food with health throughout.

Recipes avoid meat and stress simple, wholesome ingredients. Apple cookery gets many entries, from dumplings and fool to fritters and sauce. Soups, puddings, and savoury dishes follow in alphabetical order. The book reflects Edwardian interest in diet reform. It still serves cooks who want plain, meat-free Victorian and Edwardian recipes.
14004-the-every-day-life-of-abraham-linc:
Francis Fisher Browne built this life of Abraham Lincoln from the memories of men and women who had known him face to face. Published after years of planning, it favors daily scenes over grand state papers. Courtrooms, campaign trails, small-town streets, and White House rooms all appear in turn. Lincoln emerges as a neighbor first and a president second.

Anecdotes carry the argument. Friends recall his humor, his patience with callers, and his plain talk on the stump in southern Illinois, where armed crowds sometimes threatened him. Later chapters follow his wartime leadership, his pleas to the border states, and his care for popular government under strain. Readers looking for Lincoln the man, rather than Lincoln the monument, will find him here in the voices of his own circle.
14824-furnishing-the-home-of-good-taste-:
Lucy Abbot Throop's 1920 book, revised from earlier editions, sketches period styles in interior decoration and suggests how to use them in homes of today. Egypt and Greece open the survey, followed by the Renaissance in Italy and the development of decoration in France.

Louis the Fourteenth, the Regency and Louis the Fifteenth come first, then Louis the Sixteenth and the Empire. English furniture follows, from Gothic days to Queen Anne, Chippendale, Robert Adam, Hepplewhite and Sheraton. Pictures of panel spacing, pilasters and cornices show principles that fit large and small houses. Throop writes for readers who want taste with history behind it.
16019-phelim-otoole-s-courtship-and-othe:
William Carleton's Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry supplies five tales in this volume, led by Phelim O'Toole's Courtship. Phelim, an only son, inherits a snug half acre won by his grandfather Tyrrell. Tyrrell earned it with his reaping hook. A harvest trip to England brought home eight guineas, a new hat, and a staff. The family ground at Teernarogarah sets the scene.

Wildgoose Lodge, Tubber Derg or The Red Well, Neal Malone, and Art Maguire or The Broken Pledge fill out the book with courtship, crime, drink, and broken promises. Carleton's peasants talk, joke, and quarrel in lively dialect, and his stories mix comedy with moral judgment. The volume is a strong entry point to his Irish world.
16396-a-conspiracy-of-the-carbonari:
Louise Muhlbach's Conspiracy of the Carbonari, translated by Mary J. Safford and published in New York by F. Tennyson Neely in 1896, opens after Esslingen. It was the evening of May 22, 1809, a day inscribed in blood-stained letters. It brought Napoleon his first dimming of fortune. Germany, especially Austria, saw a first ray of dawn after a long, gloomy night. Tilsit, Austerlitz, and Jena had humiliated Germany, while Erfurt marked Napoleon's triumph.

From that turning point grows a tale of secret societies, patriots, and plotters working against French power. Muhlbach, author of Berlin and Sans-Souci and Frederick the Great, writes popular historical romance with sweep and feeling. Readers who like Napoleonic intrigue will enjoy this dramatic novel.
16958-the-cross-and-the-shamrock-or-how-:
An 1853 Boston tale by a missionary priest, writing under a pen name later known as Hugh Quigley, speaks straight to Irish Catholic workers in the United States. The O'Clery family faces death, the poorhouse, hard bosses, and smooth tempters, and the book tracks their trials, falls, and returns to faith. Mass in a shanty and scenes of prayer anchor the plot.

Meant both to entertain and to teach, the novel defends Catholic belief against scoff and pressure in a new land. Its long, plain chapters mix home drama with points of doctrine for servant readers. Today it reads as a vivid record of Irish immigrant life, faith, and pride in the young republic.
1831-the-lock-and-key-library-classic-my:
Julian Hawthorne edits another Lock and Key volume, this time of classic mystery and detective stories, gathering tales that defined the form. Famous names and forgotten writers share the pages. Hawthorne's classic volume gathers tales that had already proved their staying power.

The collection traces mystery from ghostly tales to logical detection, showing how the genre grew. For readers building a shelf of classic crime, this volume offers a broad, well-chosen survey. Ghost stories beside detective puzzles show mystery's two roots, fear and reason. A reader new to classic crime could start here and find the whole field.
18709-the-best-short-stories-of-1921-and:
Edward J. O'Brien edited this yearly volume at Boston with Small, Maynard and Company, after six prior years of best story picks. It gathers the best American short stories of 1921 from magazines such as the Century, the Dial, Harper's, Scribner's, and the Saturday Evening Post, with a yearbook of the American short story. Authors range from Sherwood Anderson and Ellen Glasgow to Susan Glaspell, Fannie Hurst, and Wilbur Daniel Steele.

O'Brien thanks editors and publishers for leave to reprint, and invites readers' corrections and tips. The book closes with copyright pages spanning 1920 to 1922. It serves as a snapshot of American short fiction in a single year.
19002-alice-s-adventures-under-ground-be:
Lewis Carroll published this facsimile in London and New York in 1886, reproducing the original manuscript book he had made by hand, later developed into Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. The volume carries thirty-seven illustrations by the author himself and was priced at four shillings. Its chapters follow the familiar shape in shorter form.

Alice falls down the rabbit-hole and swims in a pool of tears. She hears a long tale and takes advice from a caterpillar. Then she reaches the Queen's croquet-ground, the Mock Turtle's story, and the trial over stolen tarts. Readers get the Wonderland story at its first stage, in Carroll's own hand and pictures, a treasure for lovers of the book and for students of how it grew.
19759-address-by-honorable-franklin-k-la:
Franklin K. Lane served as Secretary of the Interior under President Wilson. This address of his deals with wartime highways transport work. It describes state committees grouped into eleven regional areas. Regional chairmen supervised those committees under the Highways Transport Committee. The Council of National Defense ran the structure. Lane's name gave the effort national weight.

Speeches by cabinet officers rallied local officials to national plans. Transport was one of the home front's hardest problems. Lane was known as a forceful, plain speaker on public questions. The address shows federal coordination reaching down to counties. It also shows how maps and regions organized the work. Such speeches are primary records of wartime administration.
20303-the-best-short-stories-of-1915-and:
The Best Short Stories of 1915 reprints the year's finest tales, with a yearbook. Permissions came from The Masses, Collier's Weekly, and many other sources. Chautonville, La Dernière Mobilisation, and The Citizen are among the tales. Editors thanked each magazine and author for the right to reprint.

A yearbook of the American short story rides with the tales. It lists stories, authors, and magazines in a useful record. Annual best volumes shaped taste and careers in fiction then. Readers get a rich cross-section of American short fiction in wartime 1915.
2038-the-lock-and-key-library-classic-my:
Julian Hawthorne edits this 1909 anthology of classic mystery and detective stories by modern English writers, including Kipling, Conan Doyle, Weyman, Collins, and Stevenson. The volume opens with Kipling's ghost story of India. Hawthorne's series appeared in 1909, when detective fiction was moving from magazines to book shelves.

Tales of murder, detection, and the uncanny follow, chosen to show the range of the form at its best. For readers new to Victorian mystery, the collection serves as a strong first shelf, with famous names beside lesser-known gems. The English volume balances famous authors with lesser tales, so a reader meets both masters and surprises.
20872-the-best-short-stories-of-1917-and:
Thanks to The Century Magazine and Scribner's fill the credits of The Best Short Stories of 1917. Edward O'Brien picked the year's finest tales for this yearly set. Thomas Beer's Onnie and Maxwell Struthers Burt's A Cup of Tea stand among the choices.

A yearbook of the American short story closes the volume with lists and notes. O'Brien tracked the field's health with charts of tales by magazine and author. Such sets guided readers to the best new fiction of the year. This one freezes 1917's story craft just as America entered the Great War.
20917-the-cultivation-of-the-native-grap:
Leif, son of Eric the Red, bought a ship and crewed it with thirty-five men in the year 1000. George Husmann quotes that old voyage in The Cultivation of the Native Grape. A German, Tyrker, sailed with Leif from Iceland in that famed crew.

Husmann, a Missouri grape pioneer, teaches vine choice, pruning, and wine making in full. Native grapes that beat rot and frost stand at his work's core. His book helped build American wine craft in the Midwest and beyond. Growers still cite his plain, tested counsel, born of decades among his own vines at Hermann.
21402-our-sailors-gallant-deeds-of-the-b:
Bold deeds by British sailors fill W. H. G. Kingston's Our Sailors, a record of the navy in Queen Victoria's reign. Kingston wrote the book early in his career and died in 1880, well before the queen. Friends brought the tale up to date after his death, with help linked to G. A. Henty.

Many of the tales are, in truth, land fights backed by naval force. Sailors hauled guns ashore and stood in the line at sieges and reliefs. The relief of Mafeking is one such famed case. The book shows how far the Victorian navy reached, on sea and land alike.
21483-the-wanderers-or-adventures-in-the:
The Macnamara family leaves Pennsylvania for Trinidad in W. H. G. Kingston's The Wanderers. Dennis Macnamara, a thriving merchant, had raised them in comfort with Uncle Paul and cousin Arthur at hand. Politics drives them out, and they choose Trinidad, a choice Kingston calls a big mistake.

Spanish priests rule the island's faith with a hard hand, and the mother's burial sparks a clash. The family flees to South America and pushes up the Orinoco River. Perils crowd the wilds there, and Spanish rule bars their way again. News of a kinder regime in Trinidad at last calls them home.
21655-the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-vol:
Volume five of Maupassant's works holds Une Vie, A Woman's Life, in a 1909 English edition. Edmund Gosse introduces the author, a Norman of old family, born at the Château de Miromesnil in 1850. Flaubert, the great Norman master, shaped the young writer's art.

Une Vie follows a woman's hopes from youth into a hard, narrowing life. Shorter tales fill the rest: Hautot Senior and Hautot Junior, Little Louise Roqué, and A Passion. Gosse notes the tales' brilliant craft and audacious tone. One tale in the French set drew threats of prosecution, which only secured the book's fortune and fame.
22091-the-best-short-stories-of-1920-and:
Edward J. O'Brien edited the yearly Best Short Stories volumes, and the 1920 book surveys stories printed in 1919. O'Brien read the magazines of America hunting for real literature among the fiction. His yearbook section lists stories, authors, and magazines in careful detail. The roll of honour names the year's finest work, judged by his strict standards.

Sherwood Anderson stands among the writers whose work the volume records. So do editors and publishers from Scribner's, Collier's, and the Cosmopolitan, thanked for their help. The series helped fix the short story's place in American letters. Libraries still use O'Brien's yearbooks to trace what the magazines printed and what one demanding editor valued.
23046-the-comedy-of-errors-the-works-of-:
A death sentence opens The Comedy of Errors in this Cambridge Shakespeare text. Merchant of Syracusa, plead no more, the Duke tells old Egeon. No partiality, the Duke rules, will bend Ephesus's laws for a Syracusan merchant. The enmity between the cities, sealed with merchants' blood, excludes all pity from our threatening looks.

Inside that grim frame spins Shakespeare's fastest farce, two sets of twins, one town, and a day of mistaken doors and dinners. Egeon's sad story gives the romp real stakes. The Cambridge edition presents the play with its scholarly notes, the fruit of collating the Folio text. Readers can watch a perfect comic machine and study how editors keep it wound. Few first plays by anyone run this cleanly.
23391-sally-of-missouri:
R. E. Young wrote this nineteen hundred three novel of Sally Madeira, a Missouri girl whose life runs from New York steering rooms to pine woods, boom towns, and the garden of dreams. Chapters trace her growth, her father's hopes, and the town Jack built, where boom time brings both fortune and folly.

Sally finds herself through work, love, and loss, as meals run out, mistakes pile up, and a sweetheart's fate hangs in the balance. Young writes with warmth and a keen eye for small town talk, mining camps, and the push of new wealth. Readers who like a heroine with grit will enjoy Sally's rise, as she learns to steer her own course through a changing West.
23445-the-best-short-stories-of-1919-and:
Edward J. O'Brien edited this yearbook of the American short story, gathering the best tales of nineteen nineteen with notes on the year's work. Earlier volumes for nineteen fifteen through nineteen eighteen had set the pattern, and this book keeps it, with copyrights from magazines and book houses across the land.

Sherwood Anderson, Djuna Barnes, James Branch Cabell, Susan Glaspell, Joseph Hergesheimer, and many more appear, their stories picked for craft and force. O'Brien's yearbook notes trace trends, praise new voices, and record where each tale first ran. Readers who love the short story will find a rich survey of a single year's best American fiction, plus a guide to the writers and journals that shaped it.
23668-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Gleeson White wrote this volume of Bell's Cathedrals series on Salisbury Cathedral, first published in December 1896 and revised with eighteen added illustrations in 1898. With fifty illustrations in all, it describes the cathedral's fabric — its stonework, plan, and fittings — and pairs that architectural account with a brief history of the See of Sarum.

Readers walk the building as White explains what they see, from the bishop's palace view to the details of nave and choir. The history places Salisbury among England's great medieval churches. It serves both visitors planning a trip and readers at home who want to understand how a Gothic cathedral was built and how its diocese grew.
24829-the-uses-of-italic-a-primer-of-inf:
Frederick W. Hamilton wrote this primer in 1918 for the Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices, issued by the United Typothetae of America. It tells young printers where italic letters came from and how to use them right, from book titles and ship names to foreign phrases and scientific terms.

The history opens with Gothic black letter, then follows smaller books and faster presses, from Gutenberg's twenty sheets an hour to the presses of 1786. Review questions close the book, testing rules for citations, footnotes, and plays. The primer remains a clear, short guide to a craft rule that still shapes printed pages.
24947-medi-val-wales-chiefly-in-the-twel:
A. G. Little's six popular lectures, published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1902, survey medieval Wales chiefly in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The opening lecture frames the theme as a failure: Wales never effected a stable and lasting political combination, and Little traces that shortfall through chronicle, castle, and cloister. Geoffrey of Monmouth and Giraldus Cambrensis receive their own lectures as the storytellers who shaped how Wales saw itself.

Castles and religious houses get full treatment, with maps and plans of Cardiff and Caerphilly among them, before the final lecture turns to Llywelyn ap Gruffydd and the Barons' War. Gerald's audience with Innocent III supplies a human touch, with the pope laughing at tales of an archbishop's bad Latin. The lectures stay clear and popular in aim, a sound entry to Welsh history.
25084-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
G. H. Palmer's Cathedral Church of Rochester, published by George Bell and Sons in 1897, is a visitor's guide to one of England's oldest cathedrals. It belongs to Bell's Cathedral series, planned to give tourists accurate, well-illustrated handbooks at a popular price without drowning them in technical terms.

Palmer describes the building stone by stone, from Gundulf's tower and the transepts to Sir George Gilbert Scott's Victorian restorations, and adds a brief history of the bishopric. The volume suits both the casual visitor walking the nave and the student of medieval architecture tracing how the fabric changed across eight centuries.
25305-memoirs-of-fanny-hill-a-new-and-ge:
John Cleland's Memoirs of Fanny Hill, first published in London in 1749, is one of the most famous and most prosecuted novels in English. This Paris edition, privately printed by Isidore Liseux in 350 numbered copies, claims a genuine text from the original.

Fanny writes letters to a friend, recalling her life from country innocence through London's underworld to love, health, and fortune. Cleland tells the story with wit and a sharp eye for manners, which is why the book survived bans and trials to become a literary classic as well as a scandal.
26367-the-young-alaskans-on-the-missouri:
Emerson Hough's 1922 boys' novel sends the Young Alaskans up the Missouri in the wake of Lewis and Clark. The boys sail in a boat named Adventurer, and Hough quotes the explorers' own orders, mess lists, and journal entries as they plan each stage. Chapters follow the river from its lower reaches toward the Platte and beyond.

Wreck, a lost hunter, and meetings with Sioux and Mandan people mark the journey, along with stops at the Yellowstone, the Great Falls, and the Three Forks. The party pushes on to the utmost source of the river, fishes for grayling, and ends at a ranch before turning home. History and outdoor adventure share the pages in equal measure.
27307-the-last-american-a-fragment-from-:
J. A. Mitchell's The Last American, a fragment from the journal of Khan-Li, Prince of Dimph-Yoo-Chur and Admiral in the Persian Navy, appeared in an edition de luxe from Stokes in 1889. It was illustrated by F. W. Read. It is dedicated to thoughtful Persians who can learn from a foolish people's swift fall after a sudden rise.

Hedful, curator of the Imperial Museum at Shiraz, presents Khan-Li's discoveries among the Mehrikan people. European comers grew flat-chested and thin, their hair scanty, their teeth fragile, and their digestions weak. Between 1945 and 1960 the last census found a sleeping continent and, in soft earth, the imprint of human feet.
28687-the-only-true-mother-goose-melodie:
Munroe and Francis of Boston published this 1833 collection of Mother Goose rhymes, claiming it as the only true text without addition or abridgement. It also promises a reliable life of the Goose family, never before published, and many illustrations. Mother Goose herself speaks in the preface, scolding rival grannies who want her soothing rhymes laid aside for more learned books.

The rhymes inside are the familiar nursery songs, presented as an anodyne for cross, peevish children who will not be comforted. This edition matters because it fixed an early American form of Mother Goose, defending nursery verse against critics who thought it too silly for children. Readers get both the rhymes and a lively piece of publishing history, in the voice of Ma'am Goose herself.
30206-humanity-s-gain-from-unbelief-repr:
Charles Bradlaugh argues that humanity has gained from unbelief, in an essay reprinted from the North American Review of March 1889. He pleads, as an unbeliever, that the slow rejection of Christianity, like the rejection of earlier faiths, has added to human happiness and well-being. Science, he says, grows from scepticism, and general progress stalls where religion forbids doubt about the supernatural.

Freethought Publishing issued the London pamphlet in 1889, and Bradlaugh writes as a Monist, using nature to mean all phenomena and all that makes any event happen. Religions, he holds, change with the peoples who hold them, and each discovery breaks some cherished belief in whole or part. Short and direct, the essay states the Victorian freethought case in its clearest form.
31384-in-the-early-days-along-the-overla:
Gilbert L. Cole's 1905 memoir, compiled by Mrs. A. Hardy and published in Kansas City, tells an overland trip through Nebraska Territory in 1852, fifty-three years before publication. Testimonials from Beatrice citizens praise it as a true story plainly told and a vivid portrayal of conditions. They call it a valuable contribution to the meager literature of a time near in years but distant in conditions.

Twelve chapters move from setting up altars of remembrance through prairies as a book, a worthy object reached for, and a snowbank's tears. They go on to stepping over the ridge, having no flag to unfurl, listening to each other, boots and saddles, and all coming right in the end. Plain and firsthand, the book preserves a pioneer's memory of the trail before Nebraska was a state.
31770-the-struggle-for-missouri:
John McElroy's 1909 history, published by the National Tribune in Washington and dedicated to the Union men of Missouri, tells how Missouri became a battleground over slavery. He argues that Southern statesmen of the elder school planned a separate government with slavery as its cornerstone, aiming to dominate the continent and absorb Cuba, Mexico, and Central America.

The book opens with Missouri's 1818 boundaries and the Ordinance of 1787, which had dedicated the Northwest to freedom. It follows the political struggle that made the state a salient bastion of the slavery empire. Readers get a partisan but detailed Civil War-era history from a Union point of view.
31974-last-days-of-the-rebellion-the-sec:
Alanson M. Randol's 1886 account Last Days of the Rebellion follows the Second New York Cavalry, Harris' Light, at Appomattox Station and Appomattox Court House on April 8 and 9, 1865. Randol, major of the First U. S. Artillery and late colonel of the Second New York, wrote from Alcatraz Island, California.

During the winter of 1864 to 1865 the regiment lay in winter quarters near Winchester, Virginia, on the Romney pike, in the first brigade, third division, cavalry corps, under General George A. Custer's division and A. C. M. Pennington's brigade. On February 27, 1865, Merritt's and Custer's divisions, with Miller's and Woodruff's batteries, all under General Sheridan, left winter quarters. Readers get a cavalry officer's account of the war's final days.
32228-the-indian-captive-a-narrative-of-:
Matthew Brayton's Indian Captive, published at Fostoria, Ohio, by the Gray Printing Company in 1896, tells of thirty-four years of captivity among the Indians of north-western America. Its first chapter, The Lost Child, sets the scene in north-western Ohio, south-east of the Black Swamp, near the end of the first quarter of the century. Hardy pioneers from New England built modest dwellings there and tilled acres won from dense forest and luxuriant prairie.

The Indians, driven from all other parts of Ohio, clung to that comparatively neglected spot, and the settler's smoke rose where the Indian wigwam stood in view. The two races were at peace, Brayton writes, for neither cared to turn a passive neighbour into an active enemy. Readers get a frontier captivity narrative, beginning with a lost child and stretching across more than three decades among the Indians.
3240-cap-n-eri:
Joseph Crosby Lincoln sets this Cape Cod novel around Captain Eri and his household. A lamb for the sacrifice opens the chapters, then the train comes in and the come-outers hold their meeting. A picture sent and a cable tested, a woman from Nantucket, and the schoolhouse bell ringing follow. Captain Eri finds a nurse, and housekeeper and book agent take their turns.

Elsie Preston, matchmaking and life-saving, heroes and a mystery, and a little politics fill the later chapters. Captain Jerry makes a mess of things before the voyage of an able seaman closes the local drama. Lincoln writes his village with affection and a keen ear. Boarding houses, town meetings, and neighbors' plans that rarely survive contact with one another carry the comedy.
32405-augusta-triumphans-or-the-way-to-m:
Andrew Moreton's pamphlet sets out a plan to make London the most flourishing city in the universe, in a second edition dated 1729 and reprinted at Oxford in 1841. Its six proposals begin with a university where gentlemen may study under the eye of their friends, a hospital for foundlings, and an academy of sciences at Christ's Hospital. Moreton also calls for closing pretended madhouses where women are unjustly confined.

Further proposals aim to save youth from ruin by clearing streets of vice, gaming tables, and Sunday debauchery. Others aim to save the lower classes from ruin by curbing the immoderate use of Geneva, or gin. The pamphlet closes with a method to prevent street robberies and a letter on the orphans' tax. It reads as a bold, practical reform tract from early Georgian London.
32548-rambling-recollections-of-chelsea-:
An Old Inhabitant's Rambling Recollections of Chelsea, transcribed from a 1901 Press Printers edition, recalls Chelsea as a village in the early part of the past century. The author, writing from Highfield Lodge, Wandsworth Common, in June 1901, compiled recollections from a diary kept only now and then, while confined to a room to pass weary hours. Friends and neighbours, he hoped, would enjoy the souvenir of old friendship.

Early Chelsea, he recalls, had village industries now entirely passed away. Villagers rode the Village Clock, a two-horse stage coach running twice daily between the Cross Keys, Lawrence Street, and Charing Cross for one shilling. A picture of the Old Swan, Chelsea, heads the volume. Readers get a warm, detailed local history of streets, shops, coaches, and neighbours before London swallowed the village.
33793-the-seven-branched-candlestick-the:
Gilbert W. Gabriel recalls the schooldays of a young American Jew in this 1925 volume, copyrighted in 1917. The narrator counts seven school years, none altogether happy but none lean: two at high school, one at a military school on the Hudson, and four at his city's university. Each year, he writes, is a lighted candle in the dark of the past, and seven together form the seven-branched candlestick, a stately and reverent symbol of his faith.

Twenty chapters move from a prologue and beginning through Friday night, the boy and the school, the military academy, a Steerforth figure, freshman year, within the gates, an aunt. The memoir blends education, identity, and coming of age with warmth and candor.
33948-the-hollow-tree-snowed-in-book-bei:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote this continuation of his Hollow Tree tales, published by Harper in 1910 with pictures by J. M. Conde. The Hollow Tree and Deep Woods people return: Mr. Crow, Mr. Turtle, Mr. Coon, Mr. Possum, Mr. Robin, Mr. Squirrel, Mr. Dog, and Mr. Rabbit. Snow shuts them in, and their winter doings fill the book.

A map of the Hollow Tree country opens the volume, with the top marked south, as the tree folk always have it. Tales of a menagerie visit and other winter scrapes follow in Paine's gentle voice. The book is a cozy winter companion to the earlier Hollow Tree volume.
34675-adventures-among-the-red-indians-r:
Adventures Among the Red Indians is a book of true tales and risks among the first folk of the two Americas, by Hyrst. He had writ past books of risks in the great woods and in the ice lands of the north. Sixteen prints fill its form.

It came out at London in the years just past, in a run of risk books of like trim at a set price. Those books are praised in its ads as a joy of their kind. A front print shows a start burst: the world seems to turn and slip from a mans feet. His head hits the boat side with a smart crack. Slow he grasps that he stands with his back to a hard thing, his frame at right bends to that of the red man in the prow.
34751-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The stretch of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, kept here runs through the letter D, and its opening pages are the transcriber's list of fixes. Those notes quote the articles they touch, and so map the ground: lives, towns, rivers, and men of science in a row.

Wilhelm Heinrich Dufour stands there, a captain in the Hundred Days, honoured later with a gift of 60,000 francs. Eugen Karl Duhring is quoted on the harmony of capitalist and labourer. Dunblane's cathedral is traced to a founding by David the First in 1141, and Pierre Dupont is shown paying seven years of exile for his songs. The river Durance closes the run kept here, spreading wide past its dykes.
34997-a-narrative-of-the-expedition-of-h:
Historical Collections of Louisiana, compiled by French, embraces translations of rare documents on that state. Natural, civil, and political history of Louisiana form the scope of the set. French supplied historical and biographical notes and an introduction to the volumes. His memberships in learned societies across the country fill the title page in the fashion of the day.

Within that frame sits a narrative of the expedition of Hernando de Soto into Florida. Early Spanish exploration of the Gulf South left few records in English dress. Translations in collections of this kind carried those records to American historians. De Soto march through the south east in the fifteen hundreds is a key event of that age. The volume preserves a primary account for students of the colonial past.
36535-antonio-stradivari:
Horace Petherick wrote a life and study of Antonio Stradivari for The Strad Library, issued at London in 1900. Petherick had served as an expert in law courts and as vice-president of the Cremona Society. His contents follow the great violin maker from birth to mastery, chapter by chapter.

First comes the master's teaching and Stradivari's slow, progressive early work, then his changes to the soundholes and the secret of his varnish against the Amati's. The true Stradivarian individuality gets a chapter, with the Long Strad and the inlaid Strads. His grand epoch, his patrons, and his assistants follow. Players and collectors who wanted the maker's whole method were the readers.
3657-wild-beasts-and-their-ways-reminisc:
Samuel White Baker writes hunting reminiscences from Europe, Asia, Africa, and America in this volume. Baker, famous for his Nile explorations, turns here to wild beasts and their ways. He describes how lions, elephants, tigers, bears, and other game live, feed, and defend themselves, and how a hunter meets them in the field. His stories span continents and decades of travel.

Baker writes as a Victorian sportsman, full of incident and practical detail about rifles, tracking, and camp life. Modern readers will note attitudes toward hunting that belong to his time. The book suits those interested in natural history, exploration, and the age when a traveler could still meet great beasts in wild country.
37049-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Clifton wrote The Cathedral Church of Lichfield for Bell's Cathedrals series, first published in 1898 and revised in this London edition of 1900, with forty illustrations. The series preface states the plan: sound, well-pictured guidebooks to the great English cathedrals at a popular price, learned enough for students yet plain enough for ordinary visitors.

Clifton thanks the standard county histories, society papers, and earlier handbooks, and names local helpers from the cathedral's own verger to the photographers whose work fills the book. His title promises two things: a description of the fabric and a brief history of the episcopal see. The series editors also point readers to fuller sources, from Britton and Willis on cathedrals to the documents printed by the Master of the Rolls. Readers get a pocket companion for walking Lichfield with informed eyes.
37130-sheffield-and-its-environs-13th-to:
Sheffield and its Environs, 13th to the 17th Century is a descriptive catalogue of land charters and other documents. T Walter Hall compiled it, and J W Northend of Sheffield printed it in 1922. The papers catalogued form the Brooke Taylor Collection and relate to the outlying districts of Sheffield. Hall dedicated the volume to the University of Sheffield.

Alongside the charter entries the book carries sixteen genealogies and an article on Hawksyard. Such a catalogue turns a private hoard of deeds into a tool any local historian can use, since each charter is described rather than merely named. Hall had already catalogued the charters in the Sheffield public reference library, and this volume extends that work to a great private collection.
38456-narrative-of-the-circumnavigation-:
Karl Scherzer, a member of the voyage, told the tale of the Austrian frigate Novara's sail round the world. The ship went out by imperial order in 1857, 1858, and 1859. Archduke Ferdinand Maximilian, chief of the Austrian navy, stood as its patron.

Commodore Wullerstorf-Urbair held command of the frigate. A chart of her track heads the book: out by Gibraltar, round to India, China, Australia, and home by the Horn. The Novara was Austria's one great reach at world science, a floating academy of naturalists and artists. Scherzer, who had travelled in Central America, writes the official tale in full: ports, peoples, plants, and trade on three oceans.
38462-narrative-of-the-circumnavigation-:
Volume two of the Narrative of the Circumnavigation of the Globe by the Austrian frigate Novara continues the official account of Austria's great scientific voyage. Dr Karl Scherzer, a member of the expedition, wrote the narrative. Saunders, Otley, and Company of London published this English volume in 1862.

The Novara sailed in 1857, 1858, and 1859 under Commodore B von Wullerstorf-Urbair, by order of the imperial government. The Archduke Ferdinand Maximilian, commander-in-chief of the Austrian navy, lent the voyage his immediate auspices. Chapter ten of this volume treats the Nicobar Islands: the arrival at Kar-Nicobar, dealings with the islanders, the village of Sáoui and its Captain John, and two white residents. Malay traders, mangrove swamps, and a boat disaster fill out the survey of Great Nicobar that follows.
38478-narrative-of-the-circumnavigation-:
Narrative of the Circumnavigation of the Globe by the Austrian Frigate Novara tells the voyage of 1857 to 1859, and this is volume three. Karl Scherzer, a member of the venture, wrote the account. Saunders and Otley published the English text at London in 1863. The Archduke Ferdinand Maximilian backed the trip as head of the Austrian navy.

Volume three opens at Sydney, already a fast growing colonial port. Scherzer praises its public buildings and its men of science. Trips inland cover wine growing, coal mines, and kangaroo hunts. The frigate goes into dry dock at Cockatoo Island for repairs. A ball on board and a serenade by local Germans close the Sydney stay. The Novara voyage was Austria's great scientific sail around the world.
38837-norman-s-new-orleans-and-environs-:
Norman New Orleans and Environs is a guide book to the city and its region, built round a short past of Louisiana. The book opens with the finding of the land and its rule by France, then Spain, then the United States. Louisiana passed from France in the sale of 1803.

Chapters then walk the city itself, with two parts on public buildings and parts on squares and trips out of town. Lists sort hotels, works, exchanges, and galleries for guests and new folk. The transcriber notes that topic breaks were added where the first book gave none. Readers get a working guide to a great river port in its prime. The book suits study of travel, trade, and city growth in the South.
39371-a-legacy-to-the-friends-of-free-di:
Benjamin Offen's 1846 Legacy addresses the friends of free discussion, laying out the main facts and persons of the Old and New Testaments, with remarks on the morality of nature. His preface defends examining the Scriptures freely.

Offen argues that free discussion destroys error and establishes truth, and he deplores the persecution of infidels and the treatment of Thomas Paine. Chapters run from the Creation to the Deluge, the confusion of tongues at Babel, and the reigns of Saul, David, and Solomon. His New Testament chapters deny the heavenly origin of Jesus and dispute the miracles and the evangelists' authenticity.
39874-an-open-letter-to-the-right-honora:
An Open Letter to David Lloyd George is a political pamphlet by Lajpat Rai, the Indian nationalist leader. Huebsch published it in New York in 1917. Rai also wrote Young India and England's Debt to India. The letter addresses the British prime minister directly. It opens with Rai presenting himself as an exile.

He writes as an Indian forced by the fear of the government in India to seek refuge in the United States. From that safety he argues India's case to the head of the British government in wartime. The letter belongs to the campaign that carried the Indian cause to American readers during the First World War.
40063-every-girl-s-library-volume-8-of-1:
Volume eight of Every Girl's Library came out in New York in 1910, edited by Percy Keese Fitzhugh. The set ran to ten volumes of reading for girls of all ages. Introductory essays came from Ella Wheeler Wilcox, Margaret E. Sangster, and Stella George Stern Perry. Each piece in the volume is paired with a short note on its author.

Inside are tales, plays, poems, and history from many hands. Readers meet Paul and Virginia, a part of Black Beauty, and scenes from Shakespeare. Poems by Shelley, Southey, Stevenson, and Tennyson sit near prose by Swift and Thackeray. The mix shows what editors of the day thought young readers should know and enjoy.
40267-the-celtic-magazine-vol-i-no-iv-fe:
The Celtic Magazine, number four, is the February 1876 issue of a monthly periodical, volume one. Its lead article concludes a study of the state of the Ossianic controversy: the long fight over whether the Ossian poems were genuine ancient works or a fabrication by their translator, Macpherson.

The writer argues from geology and geography, chiefly in the Frith of Clyde. The poems take for granted water levels far inland at Paisley, Rutherglen, and Kilsyth, as if the Clyde had stood sixty to eighty feet higher. Such an assumption, the article holds, could only come from an eye witness, not from Macpherson. The Roman Wall, found at a much lower level, is the great difficulty left to answer.
40922-pietro-ghisleri:
Marion Crawford wrote this Roman novel of Pietro Ghisleri and two step sisters. Macmillan printed it in New York and London in 1893. Chapter one says the relation of two step sisters is unusual. Mrs Carlyon came to Rome a young widow with little Laura.

Her second marriage, to Prince Camillo of Gerano, made complications there. The Prince first wife left him one child, Adele Braccio. Adele was a year and a half older than Laura Carlyon. No children were born to the Gerano couple in their union. Casa Gerano stood for years as a model household of Rome in the account.
42025-europe-in-the-sixteenth-century-14:
Europe in the Sixteenth Century, 1494 to 1598, is a history by A H Johnson in the Periods of European History series. Arthur Hassall edited the series, and this volume is its fourth period, here in a fifth edition. Johnson lectured on history at Merton, Trinity, and University Colleges, Oxford.

The series promised a trustworthy account of Europe's general development. Each volume used the latest research, pointed to original sources, and carried maps. Johnson's century runs from the French invasion of Italy to the death of Philip of Spain. Those years hold the Reformation, the wars of religion, and Spain's rise and strain. A single-volume survey had to choose its threads with care. Generations of students met the sixteenth century through books like this one. The volume shows how the period was taught before the archives were digitized.
43895-an-old-coachman-s-chatter-with-som:
Edward Corbett, a colonel late of the Shropshire Militia, wrote this book of coach-road talk. Bentley printed An Old Coachman's Chatter at London in 1890, with eight plates by John Sturgess. Corbett calls himself a semi-professional hand at the reins.

He gives the book to his old passengers of days gone by. The Royal Mails fill the first two chapters, the crack coaches of the old road. Accidents come next, then fights with snow, fogs, and floods. Corbett mixes yarns from the box seat with plain remarks on driving, as the subtitle promises. The book recalls the last bright years of the horse-drawn mail coach on English roads.
44416-a-collection-of-essays-and-fugitiv:
Noah Webster's essays and fugitiv writings on moral, historical, political, and literary subjects were printed at Boston in 1790 for the author. Webster was then an attorney at law. A French motto heads the title page. A subscribers' list follows, headed by John Adams, vice president of the United States, taking two copies, with senators of the first Congress in ranks below.

Webster, already famous for his spelling book, here shows himself as essayist of the new republic. The pieces treat the questions of a young nation: laws, manners, education, and letters. Printing for the author by subscription, with the government's first men on the list, was itself a statement. The volume stands at the start of Webster's long campaign to give America its own language and its own mind.
44480-the-loss-of-the-australia-a-narrat:
James M'Gavin, a clergyman of Dundee, edited a tale of shipwreck that Carter of New York published in 1853. Captain Adam Yule of Dundee wrote the account at the Cape of Good Hope, just after the events. In the summer of 1844 he put his large manuscript in the editor's hands. M'Gavin rebuilt the tale from those papers, keeping each great event in its place.

The brig Australia took fire on her voyage from Leith to Sydney. A list of the crew and passengers stands at the front. The chapters tell the voyage and the disaster first. Then come the sufferings in the boats and a forlorn landing. A sad march through the wilderness follows, and a rescue closes the tale. The editor kept the writer's own words of faith throughout. Fellow survivors, he says, vouched for the truth of the whole account.
44979-the-secret-memoirs-of-bertha-krupp:
Henry Fischer claims a court scoop in The Secret Memoirs of Bertha Krupp, printed by Cassell in 1916. The source, he says, is the papers and diaries of Baroness D'Alteville. She was chief gouvernante to Bertha Krupp, the arms heir. Fischer had writ on the private lives of the Kaiser and his wife.

The heads run from life under the War Lord's thumb to Bertha's fight to assert herself. She is asked to court and led to the crown prince's private room. A fortune teller sees her in a haze of blood. Plots round Archduke Franz Ferdinand fill the last heads. War era gossip fills this claim of a memoir.
45077-pubs-a-collection-of-hotel-inn-and:
Tomlin classified this gathering of pub signs, printed at London in 1922. Its full title covers hotel, inn, and tavern signs in Great Britain and Ireland, with a few foreign cafe signs added. The compiler thanks Miss Harrison for her large collection of names.

Signs are sorted by theme: farming, animals, birds, colors, fish, music, railways, and sports. Each entry gives the sign name and its town, from The Jolly Farmer at Bagshot to The Shepherd and Flock at Farnham. Notes at the end explain old signs, the highest inns, and signs painted by known artists.
45190-troy-and-its-remains-a-narrative-o:
Troy and Its Remains is an account of digging at Ilium by Henry Schliemann. John Murray published the English text in London in the year 1875. Philip Smith edited the translation, made with the author's own sanction. A map, plans, views, and cuts show five hundred objects found there. A front plate views Hissarlik from the north after the excavations.

Schliemann dug on the spot marked as Homer's Ilium by long tradition. That tradition ran unbroken from the earliest historic age of Greece. His finds of walls, gold, and pottery made world news in his day. The plain of Troy and its mounds fill his daily digging record. Scholars and the public read a treasure hunt with spades here.
45795-a-christmas-gift-to-the-american-h:
Gravengaard, once head of the Danish Evangelical Lutheran Church of America, wrote A Christmas Gift to the American Home and the Youth of America. Strandvold turned it from the Danish for the Gorham Press of Boston in 1920. Short pieces for the home make up the whole book. The full names on the title page are N P Gravengaard and G S Strandvold.

Christmas thoughts open the book, with Gravengaard recalling his boyhood Eve, his father reading from the old hymn book while his grandmother past eighty led the carols. New Year pieces follow, then talks on the worth of the soul, on prayer, on Zacchaeus, and on two events from the Civil War. One late piece hails America as the hope of the world to-day.
46306-knots-untied-or-ways-and-by-ways-i:
George McWatters, late of the Metropolitan Police in New York, wrote this account of detective life, printed at Hartford in 1871. The full title promises ways and by-ways in the hidden life of American detectives. The title page lists the company the tales keep: criminals in high life, swindlers, bank robbers, thieves, gamblers, and counterfeiters.

McWatters warns readers in his preface that not every tale is his own. Some came to him from old friends with deep knowledge of the world, and he sets theirs beside his own as pictures of human nature. The result is a set of true-seeming stories from police work, told by a man who did the job.
4631-the-hand-but-not-the-heart-or-the-l:
T. S. Arthur published The Hand but Not the Heart, or The Life-Trials of Jessie Loring, in 1858. It opens in a drawing room, where Paul Hendrickson starts at his name, a delicate flush on his handsome face, as Mrs. Denison remarks on his absent-minded air. She has watched him standing like a statue. He, assuming an indifference he plainly does not feel, denies that half an hour has passed since he came to that part of the room.

The title points to the book's trial: a hand given in marriage without the heart behind it, and the life that follows such a bargain. Arthur follows Jessie Loring through courtship, marriage, and the daily tests of affection, duty, and pride. Readers get a domestic novel of its day, earnest and readable, about what happens when the forms of love are kept while its feeling is withheld.
46607-jelly-fish-star-fish-and-sea-urchi:
Jelly-Fish, Star-Fish and Sea-Urchins is a research book by Romanes, printed at New York in 1898. It stands as volume forty-nine of the International Scientific Series. Romanes served as zoological secretary of the Linnean Society. His preface, dated London 1884, explains the book's narrow scope.

He meant at first to survey other workers on the morphology of these animals. The limits of the book made that impossible, so he kept to his own researches. The jelly-fish and star-fish are among the most beautiful and common of our seashore animals. Romanes gives their nervous systems in plain terms for the general reader, and in full detail for the working physiologist.
46818-rivers-of-great-britain-the-thames:
Rivers of Great Britain: The Thames, From Source to Sea was issued by Cassell in 1891. The book calls itself descriptive, historical, and pictorial, and this text rests on that year's edition. A view of Cliefden Woods serves as a front plate.

The first chapter, Above Oxford, is by Senior, and it starts at the river's source. Seven Springs and Thames Head open the survey, with the Churn stream and the Thames and Severn Canal. Cricklade, Castle Eaton, and Lechlade pass in turn, with the first lock on the river. Thames flowers, bird life, and weir-pools get their share of prose. Radcot Bridge and Tadpole Bridge mark the slow reaches. The whole book walks the river bank from spring to sea.
46971-surrey-painted-by-sutton-palmer-de:
Surrey is a county guide in Black's Popular Series of Colour Books. The pictures are by Sutton Palmer and the text by Hope Moncrieff. It was printed at London by A and C Black. The first edition of 1906 had seventy five illustrations. A second edition, revised, came in 1922 with thirty two. Ten chapters take the reader across the county, and an index closes the book.

The chapters begin with A Home County and The Riverside. They follow the river Wey down and the river Mole up. Then come The Pilgrims' Way, The Roman Road, Leith Hill and Hindhead. The last chapters treat Commons and Camps and The Brighton Roads. Among the home counties by London it stands first in his account. The book is a tour of that beauty in words and colour plates.
47365-a-discovrse-of-fire-and-salt-disco:
Blaise of Vigenere composed this discourse of fire and salt, printed in London in 1649 in an English rendering. The title promises many secret mysteries, both philosophical and theological. Edward Stephens gives the translation to his friend Captain Thomas Falconbridge, in a letter at the front. Stephens praises the captain's zeal for learning and truth.

The treatise takes its text from the ninth chapter of Mark, verse 49. Every man shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt. Four things are named there: man, sacrifice, fire, and salt. The opening turns to Pythagoras, held to have searched deeply into the secrets of God and nature.
48016-an-elementary-text-book-of-the-mic:
Elementary Text Book of the Microscope is a manual by J W Griffith, a London physician. Griffith was conjoint author of a standard dictionary of microscopy. Twelve coloured plates hold four hundred fifty one figures in the book. The London edition is dated eighteen sixty four. Its subtitle promises the methods of preparing and mounting objects for study.

In his preface Griffith says the book gives an elementary course in the use of the instrument. It assumes no prior knowledge of the microscope or of natural history in the reader. Descriptions of objects are kept as simple as possible, he writes. Technical terms are still added and explained, to grow familiar by degrees. The objects figured cover the main structures of plants and animals. They were chosen as common and readily procured, he adds.
48132-essays-upon-heredity-and-kindred-b:
August Weismann, professor at Freiburg, published essays on heredity and kindred biological problems in an authorised English translation at Oxford in 1889. Poulton edited the volume, with Schönland and Shipley. The author's preface explains that the essays appeared separately across seven years, on no prearranged plan.

Yet the series hangs together, Weismann says: each question grew out of the last. Reflecting on what regulates the length of life in various forms drew him on to fresh questions and further work. Some essays rest on new discoveries; others bring new points of view to well-known facts. The germ-plasm theory of heredity was taking shape in these pages.
48236-the-blood-covenant-a-primitive-rit:
Clay Trumbull wrote The Blood Covenant, a primitive rite and its bearings on Scripture, in 1885. Scribner of New York put out the book, and Trumbull had written Kadesh Barnea before it. The theme came to him while he worked on a book on friendship in the world's forces. He found facts on covenanting by the inter-transfusion of blood, and turned aside to chase them. Lectures on the rite were set for a summer school of Hebrew in Philadelphia.

Trumbull gave three lectures there on June 16, 17, and 18 of 1885, under Professor Harper of Chicago. Hearers showed such interest that he put the lectures in print, with additions. More like facts stand in an appendix at the back. The book traces one old rite through travel, history, and the Bible.
48872-woman-in-sacred-history-a-series-o:
Woman in Sacred History is a set of sketches of the women of the Bible. Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote the book, famed for a tale of the slave. It came out in New York in 1874 with fine plates in tint. The plates were made from the works of the great old hands of art.

Sarah the chief's wife heads the first group, of the first ages. Hagar the slave and Rebekah the bride stand in that group too. Leah and Rachel, the two wives of one man, close the first part. The next group takes the years of the folk as one realm. Miriam, the seer's own sister, heads that group in the list. Stowe says the gain of the book lies not in its theme. It lies in the fresh way the theme is handled in its pages.
49006-on-the-apostolical-succession-paro:
William J Irons gave lectures on the apostolical succession to a parish audience. Joseph Masters issued the second series in London in the Roman year MDCCCXLVII. Irons served as incumbent of Holy Trinity at Brompton in Middlesex. The book is given to Edward Bouverie Pusey of Oxford with warm thanks.

The lectures were preached at Saint Mary's, Newington, in Advent last, Irons writes. His aim is to clear thoughts on the source and power of the ministry. Plainness and fairness rule his statement of the argument throughout. Church readers gain a Tractarian brief told in parish-plain terms.
49036-atoms-in-agriculture-applications-:
Atoms in Agriculture, by Thomas Osborne, is an Atomic Energy Commission booklet. It stands in the Understanding the Atom series. The commission's chairman Seaborg heads its list. Osborne ran plant breeding research for the commission in Tennessee. Question and answer pages fill the book. Tracers come first: how radioisotopes track matter in soil and leaf. Plant nutrition follows, with fertilizer placement as a test case. Diseases and weeds get a section of their own. Animal nutrition asks how lean meat can be gauged on the hoof. Insects close the survey: how far they travel, how far they carry pollen.

Radiation as a tool ends the argument. It can breed new plants and kill germs, Osborne writes. A conclusion and a reference list round the pamphlet off. Plain answers serve farmers and students alike.
49814-a-correct-and-authentic-narrative-:
Captain James Barr wrote A Correct and Authentic Narrative of the Indian War in Florida. J Narine printed the book in New York in eighteen hundred thirty six. Major Dade’s massacre and starved troops fill its dread pages. The Seminole War had just burst on the young frontier state.

Powell, a bold chief, fought the tribe’s pledged move past the great river. Thompson, the agent, clapped him in irons at Fort King at first. Freed on head chief Attemottely’s bond, Powell slew his own surety. The mail man from Tampa, then Thompson himself, fell by ambush. Dade’s whole command was cut down on the march soon after. Clinch fought the host on the Ouithlacoochee in that dark month. New Orleans rose as one man to arm a relief regiment there. Seven hundred men sailed under Persifor Smith for the war.
50701-on-the-plantation-a-story-of-a-geo:
On the Plantation is a story of a Georgia boy's adventures during the war, by Joel Chandler Harris, the author of Uncle Remus. It came out in New York in 1892 from D. Appleton and Company, with twenty-three pictures by E. W. Kemble. The book is inscribed to Joseph Addison Turner, named as lawyer, editor, scholar, planter, and friend of man. Its mix of fact and tale is offered to him.

A note at the front states the author's view of his matter. Some friends who read the tales in serial form find in them more than a touch of the author's own life, he says. Be it so: it would be hard, he holds, to give the plain figure and deeds of Joe Maxwell the life that belongs to tale. Yet the lad and the events here set down seem to him born of a dream.
50736-address-centauri:
Wallace wrote a science fiction novel that Galaxy first published in 1952 under the name Accidental Flight. Doctor Cameron must give a hard answer to a man named Docchi. A council of medicine has turned down a request from a band of changed men and women, and reported its refusal to the Solar Committee.

Docchi is one of nearly a thousand such exiles. When strong feeling runs in him, his skin gives off light. Cells in his body have been altered, and his inner fire works like that of a firefly. His mates Nona, Jordan, and Anti share such gifts. They ask only that experts judge if they can crew a ship. Cameron grants that their changed bodies hold one point in their favor. Much else, he says, stands against them.
50941-motor-matt-s-enemies-or-a-struggle:
Motor Matt's Enemies, or A Struggle for the Right, is number 22 of Motor Stories, dated July 24, 1909. Street and Smith printed the weekly in New York at five cents a copy. The tale is signed only by the author of Motor Matt. A cover note shows a burning launch leaping away through thick shadows while a hoarse laugh rings out.

The cast list names Matt King as Motor Matt and Joe McGlory as his cowboy chum. George Lorry is a lad steering a wrong course, and Big John takes a dishonest toll where he can. Chapter heads promise a noose escaped, friends missing, a snare set, and a dash for the open. Fire and water both threaten the hero before the end.
52194-bob-burton-or-the-young-ranchman-o:
Bob Burton, or The Young Ranchman of the Missouri is a boys' novel by Horatio Alger, published by Porter and Coates of Philadelphia and copyrighted in 1888. Alger, author of the Ragged Dick, Luck and Pluck, and Atlantic series, dedicates the book to Plummer of Tallapoosa, Georgia, for help received in preparing it.

The contents page traces the plot in thirty-nine chapters: Aaron Wolverton steals a receipt, as the frontispiece shows, and presses scheme after scheme against the Burtons. Bob buys a ferry boat. Bob and his companions Clip and Sam are captured and escape. The trail runs to Saint Louis and a thousand dollar reward, until Brown and Minton walk into a trap. The opening scene has Bob ordering Clip to harness the colt for a drive into the village.
53358-war-to-the-knife-or-tangata-maori:
War to the Knife, or Tangata Maori is a novel by Rolf Boldrewood, author of Robbery Under Arms. Macmillan published it in London and New York in 1899. The opening chapters are set far from any battlefield. Massinger Court in Herefordshire is a grand old Tudor mansion on ten thousand acres. Its rental runs somewhat over fifteen thousand a year.

The young squire of Massinger, eight and twenty and unmarried, holds the estate by hereditary right. The narrator lingers over the great hall, its oak panelling, mullioned windows, and King Edward's corridor. Every maid and matron in the county has appraised the young man's matrimonial value. The English idyll stands at the head of a tale whose title promises the Maori wars of New Zealand, knife against knife.
54146-a-few-suggestions-to-mcgraw-hill-a:
A Few Suggestions to McGraw-Hill Authors is the publisher's handbook on manuscript preparation, issued in New York in 1922. Its subtitle promises details of manuscript preparation, typography, proof-reading, and other matters in the making of books. The house lists its technical journals at the front. They include the American Machinist, Electrical World, and Engineering News-Record.

From these journals, the preface says, the house drew its editorial guidance and marketing power. They were the natural resources behind its rapid growth. The handbook tells new authors how to prepare copy, mark proofs, and work with the house. It shows how a great technical publisher ran its book trade in the nineteen twenties.
54508-the-santa-claus-book-of-games-and-:
John Tingley of Fulton Street, New York, published this Santa Claus book of games and puzzles in 1864, promising over one hundred illustrations and a hieroglyphic preface. The preface itself is a rebus, signed by Santa Claus, who tells his young friends he hopes to combine instruction with amusement.

The contents sort the fun by kind: puzzles, charades, riddles, rebuses, enigmas, acrostics, decapitations, anagrams, and conundrums, with labyrinths scattered through the pages. One opening puzzle divides two thousand one hundred by two to show what all monkeys will readily do. Another spells a word out of a pain, a negative, a Quaker, and a vessel. Place names expressed enigmatically and cuttings for planting give older children harder work, in a book plainly made for Christmas giving.
55710-suppressed-plates-wood-engravings-:
George Somes Layard wrote a book for collectors dated 1907 about plates that were cut, held back, or changed before books reached print. Early chapters treat the suppressed portrait of Dickens and lost plates for his best known tales. Work by George Cruikshank gets close study, as do designs by Hogarth.

Later chapters turn to drawings cut from Punch and Once a Week by Charles Keene and Frederick Sandys. A case study of an Omar Khayyam etching and a long run on reused plates close the survey. Lists of plates and prints help collectors check copies and spot rare states of an image.
56354-an-appeal-to-the-people-in-behalf-:
Appeal to the People in Behalf of Their Rights as Authorized Interpreters of the Bible is a work by Catharine E Beecher. Beecher is billed as author of books on religion, domestic economy, and health. The New York edition was issued in eighteen sixty. A dedication addresses the editors of the secular press as true tribunes of the people.

The contents open with the Augustinian theory of the origin of evil. Difficulties in that theory and its place in creeds follow. Theologians themselves concede the dogmas indefensible, one chapter argues. Common sense is then defined and applied to gain the existence of God. Later chapters treat the nature of mind, its powers, its moral sense, and its will. Habit and the varieties of minds close the part shown.
57267-an-account-of-the-late-improvement:
An Account of the Late Improvements in Galvanism reports experiments with electric force on living and dead bodies. John Aldini wrote the book. He was a professor at the University of Bologna. London publishers issued it in 1803. Engravings illustrate the text. The experiments were first shown before commissioners of the French National Institute.

An appendix holds the most striking part. It gives Aldini's experiments on the body of a murderer executed at Newgate. The editor's preface calls galvanism a discovery still in its infancy. It had already drawn the keenest minds in Europe. A Turin report claimed benefit in a case of hydrophobia. The editor hopes the force may open a new field in healing.
57343-the-negro-in-chicago-a-study-of-ra:
The Negro in Chicago, a study of race relations and a race riot, was published by the University of Chicago Press under a copyright of 1922. Its author is a body, the Chicago Commission on Race Relations. The volume went to a second impression in January 1923 and a third in March. A frontispiece shows the riot's beginning: whites and Negroes leaving the Twenty-Ninth Street beach after the drowning of Eugene Williams.

The first chapter gives the riot of July 27 to August 2, 1919, in full: its background, its start, a chronological story, and the factors that fed its growth. Gangs and athletic clubs, types of clashes, crowds and mobs, and rumor each get a section. Police, militia, and deputy sheriffs follow, then the restoration of order and the aftermath.
57410-selection-from-j-a-churchill-s-gen:
Churchill of London issued a picked list from their general catalogue in March 1890, full of recent works on the art and science of medicine. The list is set, as far as can be, in the order in which medical study is pursued. It is a trade tool for students, doctors, and booksellers, not a tale.

The house notes that it prints for great bodies such as the Royal College of Surgeons and the great London hospitals. Guy's, the London, Saint Bartholomew's, Saint George's, and Saint Thomas's all have their reports and museum lists here, each with its price. The eye hospital and the mind doctors' journal close the front run of the list.
58363-sketches-of-indian-character-being:
Sketches of Indian Character surveys the traits of the North American Indians. James Napier Bailey compiled the book, printed by Hobson at Leeds in 1841. A long quote from Robertson on the study of man heads the title page. The subtitle ties the work to a saying of the socialists, that man is the creature of circumstance.

Bailey opens with that doctrine stated as plain fact. History, he writes, shows character shaped by the causes around it. Savage tribes show traits born of the savage state, he argues. Town dwellers show virtues and vices bred by town life. The Labrador native and the Londoner differ by their worlds, not their stock. Bailey then sketches Indian life to prove the rule. The book is an early British venture in the study of peoples.
58781-lives-of-famous-indian-chiefs-from:
Lives of Famous Indian Chiefs is a book by Norman Wood, out in nineteen six. Wood was a past man and speaker known for books on the black folk of the south. The book is given with thanks to the head of the United States of those days. A chief of the plains is quoted to call him the chief for red men as for white.

Lives run from a princess of the first days of the white come to the last great war chiefs. Friends of the first white towns, a red chief who built a great league, and a famed speech maker all take parts. A search past the root of the red race and tales of strife close the list. Plates drawn for the book fill its pages.
59226-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger put together an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. The file lists each book in digital form with its full contents. The Rime of the Ancient Mariner leads the list in seven parts. Biographia Literaria and the Lyrical Ballads stand among the prose and verse.

Letters in two volumes, table talk, and aids to reflection fill the range. The Complete Poetical Works come in two volumes with their own contents. Literary Remains run to four volumes at the close of the set. Readers gain a map to the wide, deep shelf of a great poet-thinker.
59351-a-history-of-domestic-manners-and-:
A History of Domestic Manners and Sentiments in England covers the Middle Ages, by Thomas Wright. Chapman and Hall published it in London in eighteen sixty two. Fairholt drew and engraved its pictures from old manuscripts and other sources. Wright dedicates the volume to the Lady Londesborough in a long letter.

That letter says histories of England leave out how our forefathers lived at home. Costume, houses, arms, and rites have their books, but manners have lacked one. Without manners, the motives and spirit of past acts cannot be rightly judged. Wright aims at plain facts in a popular form for the common reader. He grants the full subject would need all medieval letters and art surveyed. Pictures from glowing manuscripts let artists dress their figures truly at last.
59737-the-common-rocks-and-minerals-of-m:
Keller wrote this field guide, The Common Rocks and Minerals of Missouri, issued by the University of Missouri Press. A first edition came in 1945, with revised editions after, and many reprintings. Contents open with an introduction and a key for naming specimens, then walk through the state's common stones one by one.

Limestone and dolomite lead, with marble, cave onyx, and calcite near by. Shale, fire clay, sandstone, chert, agate, and jasper follow, then granite, quartz, feldspar, and mica. Ores get their share: pyrite, hematite, manganese ore, galena, and barite, closing with meteorites, gold, silver, diamonds, and uranium minerals. The introduction says the book answers the specimens Missourians mail to the university each year, asking for a name, a makeup, a worth, and a story of formation.
59789-crania-gyptiaca-or-observations-on:
Crania Aegyptiaca, or Observations on Egyptian Ethnography, by Samuel Morton, was read before the American Philosophical Society in 1842 and 1843 and printed at Philadelphia in 1844. Morton, author of Crania Americana, dedicates the work to George Gliddon, late American consul at Cairo, who supplied much of his material.

The paper asks who the ancient Egyptians were, weighing skulls from the tombs against history and the monuments. Morton sorts his finds among Jews, Arabs, Hindus, Nubians, and Negroes, and asks whether civilization rose or fell along the Nile. His race science is now discredited, but the book shaped its field for a generation.
60934-a-belle-of-the-fifties-memoirs-of-:
A Belle of the Fifties is the life tale of Mrs. Clay of Alabama, put in tale form by Ada Sterling and put out at New York in nineteen hundred and five. The rights were held in nineteen hundred and four. Plates from the face plates of the day stand in the book. The tale takes in the life of the great town and of the South from eighteen fifty three to eighteen sixty six.

The book is sworn to the dear fame of the mate of her youth, Clement Claiborne Clay, by his wife. Its first part tells of child days, girl days, and her match. Farm scenes of two south states, a great road train of the first years of the ten thirties, and the year the stars fell fill that start.
61520-the-tropical-world-aspects-of-man-:
The Tropical World is a survey of man and nature in the lands round the equator by Hartwig, the author of The Sea and Its Living Wonders. The hosted text follows the new edition of 1873, from Longmans in London. Eight coloured plates and many woodcuts fill the book.

The preface says the new edition was closely revised, with new chapters on the races of men in the tropics. The contents begin with climate. Why the tropics hold so many climates in one belt is the first question. Trade winds, the belt of calms, monsoons, and cyclones each get their due. Later chapters in the contents promise the plains of South America. Horses fight with electric eels there, and the rains turn the dry grassland into a sea of life.
61586-the-poetical-works-of-thomas-trahe:
The Poetical Works of Thomas Traherne, edited by Bertram Dobell from the original manuscripts, appeared in a second edition in 1906. Dobell published it himself at Charing Cross Road in London. A memoir of the author goes with the poems in the volume. A facsimile of a poem in Traherne own hand fronts the book as a plate.

Lines from Blake about a golden string serve as one motto for the work. A line from Wordsworth on heaven in infancy serves as a second motto. Traherne lived from about 1636 to 1674 and wrote verse of wonder at the world. His poems had rested in manuscript for more than two centuries before print. Dobell rescue of those papers gave English readers a lost voice of the seventeenth century.
61909-history-of-the-ordinance-of-1787-a:
History of the Ordinance of 1787 and the Old Northwest Territory was prepared as a supplemental text for school use. The Northwest Territory Celebration Commission issued it at Marietta, Ohio in 1937, for the one hundred fiftieth anniversary of the Ordinance. A committee of Harlow Lindley, Norris Schneider, and Milo Quaife directed the work, with the Federal Writers' Project helping.

The book was distributed free to school and college teachers in the Northwest Territory states. Other readers could buy it for ten cents, with a color pictorial map and an art copy of the Ordinance. The Ordinance of 1787 set the pattern for governing the old Northwest and for making new states from it. This text tells how the United States gained the territory and how the states developed from it.
61956-the-early-irish-monastic-schools-a:
Hugh Graham studied Ireland's gift to early medieval culture through its monastery schools. The Talbot Press issued The Early Irish Monastic Schools at Dublin in 1923. Graham taught education at the College of St Teresa in Winona, Minnesota. The book is given to Irish teachers in many lands.

Seven chapters run from pagan learning to the scope of Irish scholarship. A quote from Dr Samuel Johnson calls Ireland the school of the West. Five hundred and thirty-nine footnotes, moved to the back, ground the tale. Students gain a proud, sourced account of learning kept alive in dark times.
62282-across-the-vatna-jo-kull-or-scenes:
Across the Vatna Jokull is an Iceland roam book by William Lord Watts. A Longmans house of London brought it out in eighteen seventy six. Its next name calls it scenes in Iceland, of lands not yet known. Watts gives the book to his Icelandic friends in its front leaves. Mount Paul stands as front plate of the print in its cut list.

His front word owns he crossed tracts of which naught was known ere then. Fire mounts in the north of the isle stand in that same word. Back in Reykjavik on the same quest as in past years, he opens. Some at home call such trips fool hard and folly, he owns at start. Two maps trace his roads from town to town in the print scheme.
62973-building-and-flying-an-aeroplane-a:
Building and Flying an Aeroplane is a practical handbook on the design, construction, and operation of aeroplanes and gliders, issued in 1912 for the American School of Correspondence. Its two parts move from building models and a glider to full machines: a Curtiss biplane in the first part and a Blériot monoplane in the second. Examination papers close each part for students earning credit.

Chapters on details of construction, the art of flying, and accidents and their lessons teach by measurements, drawings, and hard experience.
