The frontispiece shows a twenty-horsepower Nieuport monoplane making a landing. Written when flight was barely nine years old, the handbook records a moment when any handy reader could dream of building a machine in a barn and flying it.
62993-the-handy-horse-book-or-practical-:
The Handy Horse-Book, by a cavalry officer, reached a fourth edition, revised and enlarged, with engravings. Its full title promises practical instructions in driving, riding, and the general care and management of horses, and the front pages are given over to opinions of the press.

Bell's Life calls the title no misnomer. The Athenaeum says the author writes as cavalry officer, hunting horseman, coach proprietor, whip, and steeplechase rider, giving the cream of his information. The Observer adds that he renders horse-proprietors independent of ignorant farriers and grooms, and the Irish Times calls the book a multum in parvo.
63396-the-geologic-story-of-the-great-pl:
A geology bulletin by Donald E Trimble, published at Washington in 1980. It is Geological Survey Bulletin 1493. The subtitle calls it a nontechnical description. Its subject is the origin and evolution of the Great Plains landscape. A Denver photograph and a long Pike quotation open the front matter. Pike doubted the prairies could ever be cultivated.

Trimble first defines the Great Plains and their parts. Early history, warping, and stream deposition follow. Sculpturing the land explains how the surface was carved. Today's landforms fill the later chapters: Black Hills, High Plains, Missouri Plateau. Library cataloguing data and an index support the text. The Survey sold such bulletins cheaply to the public. Trimble writes for ranchers, teachers, and travellers, not specialists.
65855-the-bloody-theatre-or-martyrs-mirr:
The Bloody Theatre, or Martyrs Mirror of the Defenseless Christians, was compiled by Thieleman van Braght and put into English by Joseph Sohm. The English text comes from the Dutch edition of 1660. Its full title states the scope in detail.

The Christians it honours were baptised only upon confession of faith. They suffered and died, it says, for the testimony of Jesus, their Saviour. The span runs from the time of Christ to the year 1660. Braght drew the accounts from many true chronicles, memorials, and testimonies. Pictures have been moved in this text to sit near the words they belong to. Readers get the great Anabaptist martyrology, a vast record of faith held under torture and death.
67370-from-missouri:
Zane Grey wrote this western novelette, complete in one magazine issue, with paintings by Frank Street. Tex stalks out of the post-office with a letter and rounds on his three comrades: which of them has written to her again?

The handwriting is from Missouri, and the letter is addressed to Mr Frank Owens at Springer's Ranch, Beacon, Arizona. The joke dawns: Frank Owens is all of them. The outfit had read of a Kansas City schoolteacher wanting a job in dry Arizona, and had written to lure her out, swearing none would write again. Now she has written back unasked. Grey builds the tale on cowboy honor and a schoolmarm en route. Readers get his Arizona in miniature.
68178-joel-chandler-harris-life-of-henry:
Joel Chandler Harris' Life of Henry Grady is a memorial volume published by Cassell in 1890. Grady's co-workers on The Constitution newspaper compiled it. Harris, famous as Uncle Remus, edited the whole. The volume was sold only by subscription, for the benefit of Grady's family and mother. A dedication looks to the lofty purpose that guided their messenger of peace. Peace and unity between North and South receive the dedication.

Henry Watterson contributes the opening In Memoriam piece. Harris himself writes the biographical sketch of some sixty pages. A memorial sketch by Marion Verdery follows. Then come Grady's writings and speeches themselves. The New South speech, given at a New England Club banquet, heads the list. Grady's fame as the South's spokesman rests on such addresses.
68385-civilization-in-the-united-states-:
Civilization in the United States, an Inquiry by Thirty Americans, was edited by Harold Stearns and published in New York in 1922. Thirty writers each take one part of American life. Lewis Mumford writes on the city, Mencken on politics, and John Macy on journalism.

Other essays cover law, education, scholarship, school and college life, and science. Brooks writes on the literary life, Taylor on music, Aiken on poetry, and Nathan on the theatre. Later pieces treat the small town, history, sex, the family, the alien, business, medicine, sport, and humour. Lardner writes on sport and play. Readers get a broad, sharp survey of the United States just after the First World War, by many hands and in many voices.
68741-ancient-rome-in-the-english-novel-:
Randolph Faries the Second wrote Ancient Rome in the English Novel. The University of Pennsylvania took it as his thesis in 1923. Lyon and Armor printed it at Philadelphia. Definition of the Field opens the study. Important Novels of Roman Life stand listed there. Genesis of the Roman novel fills chapter two.

The first true novel of Roman life gets named. Vathek's influence on that line gets weighed. The Byronic romance's pull stands next in line. A fully developed form closes that chapter. Development lines run from 1834 to his day. Great preachers' scholarship marks one such line. Becker's Gallus set a standard of detail, he notes. German followers of Scott fill another line. Pedantic and popular novels divide the field late. A doctoral map of Roman fiction sorts saints' tales, school tales, and melodrama into one learned family tree.
69184-travels-in-western-australia-being:
Travels in Western Australia is a descriptive tour by May Vivienne. The hosted text opens with press opinions of the first edition. The Daily Chronicle calls Vivienne a delightful and exhilarating guide. Her book tells what somebody really saw and felt, it says. The Empire Review praises its first hand information. Cities, goldfields, and agricultural districts are clearly given.

The Financial Times ranks it among the most entertaining books on the colony. The Pall Mall Gazette says Vivienne knows her Westralia up and down. She visited farms and timber estates and inspected the chief mines. She pegged a claim with her own hand. The pioneer fringe of civilisation did not stop her travels. A portrait of John Forrest, the statesman, stands among the illustrations. The book doubles as travel record and work of reference.
70646-ludus-coventri:
Ludus Coventriae is a collection of mystery plays edited by James Orchard Halliwell. The Shakespeare Society printed it in London in 1841. Its title page calls it mysteries formerly represented at Coventry. They were played on the feast of Corpus Christi there. The council of the Shakespeare Society fills the front pages. The Marquess of Normandy presided over that society. Lords Braybrooke and Leigh served as vice presidents. Collier directed the society's work in those years. An illustration plate stands at the front of the volume.

An introduction begins by noting three complete things, in the cut text. The cycle dramatizes Bible history in English verse plays. Townsfolk once performed such cycles in the streets on feast days. The Shakespeare Society printed old drama for scholars and actors. This volume preserves a whole Corpus Christi cycle in print.
71989-the-salabue-stradivari:
The Hill firm of London wrote The Salabue Stradivari in 1891, a life and close study of a famed violin. The trade knows the piece as Le Messie, and the book bears three plates in color by Shirley Slocombe. It is the second in a line of such works, after one on the Tuscan Stradivari. The Hills say they sought facts from first sources and sifted proof with care. Federico Sacchi of Cremona helped them hunt down points that had long been dim.

Inside, the book sets out the traits of the violin and tests them part by part. Robert Harrison shaped the mass of notes into one memoir. The firm drew on more than fifty years of craft skill and trade lore. For fans of fine fiddles, the book fixes hard facts about one prized work of Stradivari.
72016-a-practical-treatise-on-coach-buil:
A Practical Treatise on Coach-Building, by James Burgess, was published in London in 1881. Fifty seven pictures go with the text. Burgess says the trade had lacked a full book for some fifty years. Makers kept rich notes but did not print them. Apprentices and others thus had no way to learn the craft. His aim is general use, not fine points alone. He stresses the rules behind sound building over fixed sizes.

Chapter one traces vehicles from raft and sledge to modern forms. The reader then enters the workshop with the designer and draughtsman. Drawing a carriage comes before building it. Later matter gives hints on the proper keeping of carriages. The book serves both the history fan and the working coach builder.
72054-motion-pictures-1974-catalog-of-co:
Volume twenty eight of the Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, parts twelve to thirteen, number one, covers motion pictures. It lists entries for January to June in nineteen seventy four. The Copyright Office of the Library of Congress issued the volume at Washington in nineteen seventy four. Front pages give the key title of the series and explain how the whole catalog is divided into parts.

Books and pamphlets, periodicals, dramas, music, and maps each have their own part. The pages also explain the class letters used for published and unpublished works. The body of the volume is the motion picture list itself, the half year record of films entered for copyright. Film researchers get the official registration record for American motion pictures in the first half of nineteen seventy four.
73714-journals-of-conrad-weiser-1748-geo:
Early Western Travels opens with this volume of journals from the years 1748 to 1765, edited by Reuben Gold Thwaites and printed at Cleveland in 1904. The series reprints rare old books of travel that describe Native peoples and settler life in the middle and far West. Thwaites added notes, introductions, and an index to each text.

Conrad Weiser's journal of a tour to the Ohio in 1748 comes first. George Croghan's letters and journals follow, covering tours into the western country from 1750 to 1765, talks with Native nations, and a treaty at Logstown. Writings by Christian Frederick Post from 1758 and Thomas Morris from 1764 complete the volume.
74303-the-baz-nama-yi-nasiri:
The Baz-Nama-yi Nasiri is a Persian treatise on falconry in English dress. Colonel Phillott made the translation, issued at London in 1908. Only five hundred copies were printed by Quaritch. Phillott served the Asiatic Society of Bengal at Calcutta. The author was a Persian prince, Timur Mirza. He was one of nineteen sons of a governor of Fars. A painting of hawking fronts the book.

The dedication recalls days spent with a Persian grandee in exile. Phillott and his friend had wept together in a garden, he says. The translator's opening tells of the author's royal house. Falconry was a high art at the Persian court. A full manual of it joins lore to practice. Such books kept the terms and rules of the sport. Phillott's version made the craft open to English readers.
7485-the-last-american-a-fragment-from-t:
J. A. Mitchell's satire of 1889 imagines America extinct and explored by Persians. The fragment is presented as the journal of Khan-Li, prince of Dimph-Yoo-Chur and admiral in the Persian navy, introduced by Hedful, curator of the Imperial Museum at Shiraz. The explorers find the ruins of a people who rose suddenly and vanished swiftly, and the book is dedicated to thoughtful Persians who can read a warning in that fate.

Mitchell uses the future explorer's eye to satirize his own age: its nervous energy, its imitation of other nations, its extravagance, and its thin patriotism, as the Persian narrator judges them. The satire bites because the ruins are familiar: American cities, customs, and boasts seen through foreign eyes. The Last American is an early work of future-history fiction, funny and sharp.
74885-motion-pictures-1975-catalog-of-co:
Motion Pictures 1975 is one part of the Catalog of Copyright Entries, third series, from the Copyright Office of the Library of Congress. The volume is number 29, parts 12 and 13, number 1. It covers films filed from January to June 1975 and was printed at Washington in 1976.

Front pages explain the scheme of the whole catalog. Signs mark works as in print or not, and each part has its price per half year issue. Books, music, drama, and maps each have parts of their own. This part lists film claims in order for search by makers, lawyers, and film men. It is a plain tool book, made for daily use at a desk.
74957-indian-sketches-taken-during-an-ex:
Indian Sketches is John Irving's account of an expedition to the Pawnee tribes, and this text is volume two of two. Carey, Lea and Blanchard published it at Philadelphia in 1835. An errata list corrects Pawnee names through the volume. The first chapter tells of preparations for reception by the Grand Pawnees.

Half-breed scouts sent out by the commissioner came in during the evening with promises of a friendly welcome. At sunrise the tents were struck and loaded on the heavy baggage wagons. Irving, the son of Washington Irving, travelled with the dragoon expedition to the plains. His sketches record Pawnee councils, hunts, and ceremonies as an eyewitness of 1835.
76210-roughing-it-in-siberia-with-some-a:
Robert Jefferson, who had crossed Siberia on a bicycle, wrote Roughing It in Siberia, published in London by Sampson Low in 1897. The subtitle adds the book's business: the Trans-Siberian Railway, and the gold-mining industry of Asiatic Russia. His portrait fronts the volume.

The chapters follow his route east. The first day in Asia and arrival at Omsk open the road. He crosses the steppe and the Ob valley to Tomsk, reaches the end of the railway, and sails down the Yenesei. Two chapters inspect Siberian gold mining and life at the mine. A trip into China closes the book. British readers of 1897 got the great railway half built and the gold fields beyond it.
76427-the-best-short-stories-of-1922-and:
Edward O'Brien edited The Best Short Stories of 1922 and the Yearbook of the American Short Story, published by Small, Maynard and Company in Boston. O'Brien had edited the annual series since 1915. Each year he chose the best stories from the magazines and added a yearbook of the field.

The copyright pages list the year's chosen authors. Conrad Aiken, Sherwood Anderson, and Konrad Bercovici appear, along with Scott Fitzgerald, Ben Hecht, and Joseph Hergesheimer. Ring Lardner, James Oppenheim, and Wilbur Daniel Steele round out the list. O'Brien's annuals mapped the rise of the American short story between the wars. His choices, arguments, and rolls of honor gave young writers a standard to aim at and readers a guide through the flood of magazine fiction.
76917-ida-nicolari:
Ida Nicolari, by Eglanton Thorne, was published in London by the Religious Tract Society. Thorne had also written The Old Worcester Jug, It All Real True, and In London Fields. Contents list twenty five chapters of studio and family life.

Psyche opens, then her mother friend, and the sculptor pupil. Geraldine Seabrook, a sore dread, and visitors to the studio follow. Ida begins to know herself, and a visit from Theodore Tregoning, come next. Chapters named blind and patient endurance mark the crisis. A wedding day draws near. Chapter one opens in a studio, with a model released as the light fails. Readers get a Tract Society tale of art and faith.
77328-the-best-short-stories-of-1925-and:
The Best Short Stories of nineteen twenty-five is the annual anthology edited by Edward J O'Brien, who had run the series since the volume for nineteen fifteen. Each year O'Brien read the magazines, chose the finest American stories, and bound them with a yearbook of the American short story.

The front matter lists O'Brien's shelf of earlier volumes, from White Fountains and The Forgotten Threshold to a decade of these yearly collections. Their British companions were edited with John Cournos. The yearbook side of the annual graded magazines and stories and tracked the form's health, which made the series a working tool for writers and editors. The nineteen twenty-five volume is one link in the chain that defined the American short story between the wars.
79283-mata-hari:
Thomas Coulson wrote the life tale of Mata Hari, dancer and spy. The book came out in New York and London in 1930. Plates come from the store of Adolphe Roberts. Coulson was a major with a state award to his name. He gave the book to Mitsou in its front pages.

Her wild road stirred rare pity for a spy, he notes. Spies draw hate from foes and shy praise from the rest, he says. Yet princes, state men, and scholars spoke up for this stage star. Why she won such guards is his book's first ask. Her dance fame and her dire end frame the whole tale.
79369-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Cathedral Church of Southwell is a guide monograph by Arthur Dimock, issued by George Bell and Sons in 1898. It belongs to the Bell Cathedrals series of handbooks for the great English cathedrals. The book holds thirty eight illustrations, and a photograph shows Southwell from the west at its front. Its full title promises a description of the fabric and a brief history of the episcopal see.

A general preface states the aim of the series for its readers in plain terms. The monographs were planned to supply visitors with accurate, well illustrated guide books at a popular price. Each writer was to write with knowledge enough for the student of archaeology and history in his work. Southwell, the minster of Nottinghamshire, gets that treatment here: its Norman nave, chapter house leaves, and bishops set out for the visitor with a plan in hand.
79656-the-best-short-stories-of-1916-and:
The Best Short Stories of 1916 is an anthology edited by Edward O'Brien, published in Boston by Small, Maynard in 1917. A yearbook of the American short story is bound with the chosen stories. The volume is dedicated to Richard Matthews Hallet.

Long copyright pages list the magazines that first printed the stories. The Atlantic Monthly, Harper's, Scribner's, The Century, and The Seven Arts are among them. Authors named in the permissions include Gertrude Atherton, Theodore Dreiser, Fannie Hurst, and Wilbur Daniel Steele. O'Brien made his annual volumes a record of the short story's standing in America. The yearbook sections tracked magazines, writers, and trends year by year. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
a-conspiracy-of-the-carbonari: Luise Muhlbach tells of a conspiracy of the Carbonari after the battle of Essling. The novel opens on the evening of May 22, 1809, the day that first dimmed Napoleon's star. A father shows his daughter Leonore ten banknotes of fifty thousand francs each, calling them magic spells. Muhlbach weaves secret societies, money, and Napoleonic politics into a historical romance.
alice-s-adventures-under-ground-being-a-: Lewis Carroll presents a facsimile of his original manuscript book, Alice's Adventures Under Ground, later developed into Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. The hand-written text, with thirty-seven of the author's own illustrations, shows the tale in its first, shorter form. It is a treasure for Carroll lovers, revealing how a story told to a child grew into a classic.
amos-kilbright-his-adscititious-experien: Frank R. Stockton tells of Amos Kilbright and his adscititious experiences, with other stories including a reversible landscape and dusky philosophy in two expositions. Stockton's humour turns on odd notions taken to their logical end, with a light, inventive touch. The collection shows why he was a favourite maker of American comic tales.
an-enquiry-concerning-the-principles-of-: Frances Reynolds enquires into the principles of taste and the origin of our ideas of beauty. Her essay argues about how we judge what is fine, and where our sense of beauty comes from. As a woman theorist of art in the eighteenth century, Reynolds offers a rare, thoughtful voice on aesthetics.
an-unwilling-maid-being-the-history-of-c: Jeanie Gould Lincoln tells the history of certain episodes during the American Revolution in the early life of Mistress Betty Yorke, born Wolcott, an unwilling maid. The chapters follow Miss Moppet, bullets for defence, and Oliver's prisoner, as a girl meets war with spirit. Addressed to a nineteenth-century girl, the book makes history personal and lively.
b09-melanchthon-de-obitu-lutheri:
De obitu Martini Lutheri is the funeral oration Philipp Melanchthon gave for Martin Luther at Wittenberg. Luther died in February 1546, and Melanchthon spoke over him on February 19, before the gathered university and town. The Latin oration served as the Reformation's public farewell to its founder.

Melanchthon traces Luther's life, teaching, and trials, and praises the gifts God gave the church through him. Grief runs through the speech, held in check by a scholar's order. The text also fixes an early, near account of how Luther's own circle wished him remembered. It remains a moving close to the first age of the Reformation.
britannica-1911-a-fortiori: A fortiori, a Latin phrase meaning from a stronger reason, names a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry defines an argument that proves a point through a stronger case that already covers it. If A is shown less than B, and A is known greater than C, then C falls below B with no fresh proof. Where the ground is only likelihood, as in the Gospel saying the entry cites, the move rests on common sense rather than strict proof.
britannica-1911-a-priori:
A priori, from what comes before, receives a compact entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the phrase two lives: common speech for a judgment made without fresh facts, and logic, where Albert of Saxony first used it. Aristotle's order of cause and effect stands behind both.

Nature puts causes first, while human learning starts from facts, the entry explains. Kant recast the pair as kinds of judgment: a priori, free of sense reports, and a posteriori, drawn from them. Camps of Intuitionalist and Empiricist fought over the line. The entry ends in truce: pure a priori thought is form without content, and all real knowing mixes mind with fact.
britannica-1911-abba-mari:
Abba Mari receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abba Mari ben Moses, called Astruc of Lunel, was a French rabbi born near Montpellier late in the thirteenth century. Talmud, Maimonides, and Nachmanides formed his learning, in a house of learned men.

At Montpellier he fought the spread of Aristotelian reason drawn from Maimonides, fearing for law, miracle, and revelation. His letters, gathered as Minhat Kenaot, called Solomon ben Adret of Barcelona to orthodoxy's aid. A ban on philosophy study under age thirty followed in 1305, and schism followed the ban. Driven from France in 1306, he settled at Perpignan and printed the letters. Verse and civil law works stand to his name as well.
britannica-1911-abu-l-ala-ul-ma-arri:
Abu-l-'Ala ul-Ma'arri (973-1057) was an Arabian poet and letter-writer from Ma'arrat un-Nu'man in Syria, south of Aleppo. Blinded by smallpox at the age of four, he still studied under leading teachers at Aleppo, Antioch, and Tripoli. A stay in Baghdad brought him into its literary circles before he returned home to teach and write.

Two collections of poems and two of letters carry his name. The later poems, the Luzumiyyat, use a hard double-consonant rhyme and turn pessimistic, reflecting on change, virtue, and death. His letters treat literary and social subjects, and one set deals with his vegetarian views. Readers meet a blind scholar whose memory and independence set him apart.
britannica-1911-aiyar-sir-sheshadri:
Sheshadri Aiyar is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a statesman of Mysore in India, born in eighteen forty five. He was schooled at Calicut and at Madras and joined state service as a translator. In time he moved to Mysore and rose through post after post.

The entry tells how he became chief minister of the state in eighteen eighty five. For the next span of years he drove works to enrich the land. Rail lines, water works, and mines all grew under his hand. The wealth of the state rose and its funds were set on a sound base. He left office in nineteen hundred with a high British honour.
britannica-1911-arnaud-henri:
Henri Arnaud (1641-1721), pastor and general of the Waldensians of Piedmont, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Embrun, he went back with his family about 1650 to their home valley. He was schooled there, then at Basel and at the academy in Geneva. He came home and served as pastor in several valleys of his people.

The article makes him the natural leader of his faith when the Duke of Savoy drove them from their valleys in 1686. He gathered some three thousand exiles in Switzerland and sought help in Holland, where William of Orange gave money and aid. Twice the exiles tried and failed to regain their homes. The English revolution of 1688 fired a third try. In August 1689 Arnaud set out with about a thousand followers, guided by written plans from an aged veteran.
britannica-1911-bakhtiari:
Bakhtiari are one of Persia's great nomad tribes. Their camping grounds fill a hilly province. It runs from Chaharmahal toward Shushter. The Dizful river bounds it northward. Behbahan and Ram Hormuz touch it southward. Two great divisions split the tribe.

Haft-lang and Chahar-lang are those divisions. Many branches and clans follow them. Until the 1400s they were the Great Lurs. Their speech is the Lur language. It is a Persian dialect. They number some 38,000 to 40,000 families. That means under 200,000 souls in all. Their district covers about 25,000 square miles. Mid-century they could field 20,000 horsemen. Feuds and misrule have shrunk that strength. Perhaps 4,000 horsemen remain available now. Their chiefs lately improved the Isfahan road. Iron bridges now cross the Karun there.
britannica-1911-bakri:
Bakri (1040-1094) was an Arabian geographer of Spain. His full name runs Abdallah ibn Abd ul-Aziz ul-Bakri. Cordova was his birthplace and home. His best-known work is a dictionary of names. It covers geographical names found in the poets. Such names often puzzle readers of old verse.

An introduction treats the Arabian tribes' seats. It sets out where each tribe lived. Wüstenfeld edited the dictionary at Göttingen. The edition ran through 1876 and 1877. Another work was a general world geography. That book survives only in manuscript form. Its North Africa part was edited separately. De Slane published it at Algiers in 1857. Brockelmann's history of Arabic literature gives more detail. It treats Bakri among the geographers of his age.
britannica-1911-balikisri:
Balikisri, also spelled Balukiser, was a town of Asia Minor, chief town of the Karasi sanjak in the vilayet of Brusa. It stands 575 feet up, on rising ground above a fertile plain that drains toward the Sea of Marmora. Its people numbered about 20,000, most of them Moslems, with some 5,000 Christians.

Trade in opium, silk, and grain centred on the town, linked by carriage roads to Panderma. The 1911 Britannica entry notes silver mines worked at Balia and boracite mines at Susurlu, signs of the district's mineral wealth. On or near the site stood the Roman town of Hadrianutherae, founded by the emperor Hadrian.
britannica-1911-beri-beri:
Beri-beri is a tropical disease of the greatest age, known to the Chinese from very early times. It faded from European sight until an outbreak in Brazil in 1863 and study in Japan and Borneo brought it back. Work by Scheube and Bälz in Japan and by Pekelharing and Winkler in the Dutch Indies described it as a form of peripheral neuritis, a wasting of the nerves.

The disease ranges between 45 degrees north and 35 south: Japan, Korea, the China coast, Burma, Java, Ceylon and East Africa, and across to Cuba, Panama and South America. Ships have carried it as far as Australia and London. Many authorities of the day blamed an infective parasite, though none had been surely found; the young, from fifteen to forty, suffer most.
britannica-1911-bihari:
Bihari is the most western of the four languages in the Eastern Group of modern Indo-Aryan tongues. The others are Bengali, Oriya, and Assamese. The 1911 Britannica article, signed by Grierson, counts 34,579,844 Bihari speakers in British India in 1901. The whole group then numbered over ninety million. Bihari is also spoken in the Tarai districts of Nepal. Its name means the language of the province of Bihar.

The article traces Bihari to the old Magadhi Prakrit of South Bihar. It maps the speech far beyond the province, west past Benares and south over Chota Nagpur. Dialects such as Bhojpuri and Magahi get detailed treatment. Grammar, sounds, and literature are worked through at great length. Long lists of authorities close the piece. It is a technical survey for language students, not a general sketch.
britannica-1911-bolgari:
Bolgari, or Bolgary, is a ruined town in the Russian government of Kazan, 4 miles from the left bank of the Volga. It is generally taken to have been the capital of the Bulgarians in that region from the 400s to the 1400s. Old walls and towers still stand on the site.

Burial mounds around it hold inscriptions in Arabic, Armenian, and Turkic, and dug tombs gave up weapons, tools, dishes, and silver and copper coins. Finds gathered from 1722 sit in museums at Kazan, Moscow, and St Petersburg. Mongols wrecked the city in 1238 and Tamerlane wrecked it again a century later. It then served the khans of the Golden Horde before passing to the principality of Kazan in the late 1400s.
britannica-1911-boulainvilliers-henri:
Henri, comte de Boulainvilliers (1658–1722), was a French political writer who praised the feudal order without reserve. Born at St Saire in Normandy and schooled at Juilly, he served in the army until 1697. All his books came out after his death, among them histories of France's old government and of the peerage, and a history of the Arabs.

He was an aristocrat of the strongest type, the entry says, attacking absolute monarchy on one side and popular government on the other. He worked hard to prove his own family's ancient nobility and held that rule should rest solely with men of his class. His Histoire de l'ancien gouvernement de la France and his État de la France, both printed in 1727, carried his feudal argument across Europe. He died in Paris in 1722.
britannica-1911-brisson-eugene-henri:
Eugene Henri Brisson (born 1835) was a French statesman born at Bourges on 31 July 1835. Trained as an advocate like his father, he stood out in opposition during the last days of the empire and became deputy-mayor of Paris after its fall. Voters sent him to the Assembly on 8 February 1871 as a member of the extreme Left.

He backed obligatory primary schooling and fought clerical power, and he was first to propose an amnesty for the condemned of the Commune in September 1871, though the vote went against him. President of the chamber from 1881 to March 1885, he succeeded Jules Ferry as prime minister, then resigned after barely winning a credit vote for the Tongking expedition. Later he helped expose the Panama scandals, nearly won the presidency after Carnot's murder in 1894, and headed a cabinet in June 1898 amid the Dreyfus affair.
britannica-1911-buccari:
Buccari is a royal free town of Croatia-Slavonia, in Hungary. Its Serbo-Croatian name is Bakar. It stands seven miles south-east of Fiume. The town sits on a small bay of the Adriatic Sea. Its population in 1900 was 1870. This 1911 Britannica entry describes its trade and harbour.

The harbour gives good anchorage to small vessels. Its approach can be dangerous, though. Rivalry from Fiume cost Buccari most of its trade in the 19th century. Boatbuilding is now the staple industry. A coasting trade runs in fish, wine, wood and coal. The tunny fishery also brings in money. The state railway ends about two and a half miles away. Near the town stands the old castle of Buccarica. Farther south lies the small port of Porto Ré, or Kraljevica.
britannica-1911-bukhari:
Bukhari (810-872), an Arabic author, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He made the most widely accepted gathering of traditions about Mahomet. Born at Bokhara, of an Iranian family, he showed an early gift for learning traditions by heart. At sixteen he made the pilgrimage to Mecca with his family and gathered more matter on the way.

The article says that by eighteen he had given himself to gathering, sifting, testing, and setting in order the traditions. For that work he travelled over the Muslim world, from Egypt to Samarkand. The tale runs that he learned three hundred thousand traditions, true and false, from more than a thousand men. He became the known master of the field. His power and speed of memory seemed a marvel even to his own age. After sixteen years away he went home to draw up his great book.
britannica-1911-cagliari:
Cagliari is the subject of a city entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the island of Sardinia and chief town of its province. That province covers the southern half of the island. Population figures for town and commune in nineteen hundred are both given in the entry.

It is finely set at the north end of the Gulf of Cagliari, in the centre of the south coast. The medieval town fills a long narrow hill with steep cliffs on each side. That hill must have been the ancient stronghold, the entry says. The modern town, like the Roman town before it, spreads down the slopes.
britannica-1911-capri:
Capri is an island on the south side of the Bay of Naples. Its ancient name was Capreae. This 1911 Britannica entry describes it in detail. It lies about 20 miles south of the town of Naples. It forms part of the province of Naples. The commune of Capri held 3890 people in 1901. Anacapri, the second town, held 2316. The island is 4 miles long and covers 5.5 square miles.

Monte Solaro, the highest point, rises 1920 feet. The east cliffs drop 900 feet sheer to the sea. The only safe landing is on the north side. Two towns, Capri and Anacapri, stand at different heights. A flight of 784 steps joined them until 1874. A carriage road then replaced the climb. The island lacks water and is dusty in drought. Still, it yields fruit, wine and olive oil. Some 30,000 visitors came each year, drawn by the scenery.
britannica-1911-carbonari:
The Carbonari were secret revolutionary societies in Italy and France. Their name is Italian for “charcoal-burners.” This long 1911 Britannica article traces their history. They played an active part early in the 19th century. Stories linking them to medieval brotherhoods are pure fancy. The entry calls those tales fantastic and dismisses them. The Carbonari were probably an offshoot of the Freemasons.

They first gained weight in southern Italy. That was during the Napoleonic wars in Europe. Under Murat's reign, from 1808 to 1815, secret societies multiplied. Their aim was to free Italy from foreign rule. They also sought constitutional liberties for the people. They would back the Bourbons or Murat, if either delivered. Their watchwords were freedom and independence for Italy. But they agreed on no single form of government. The article follows their plots, risings and suppression in turn.
britannica-1911-carthage-missouri:
Carthage is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city and the county-seat of Jasper county, Missouri, on the Spring river about 150 miles south by east of Kansas City. Its population was 9483 in the census of 1910. Three railways serve the city, and an electric line links it with Webb City, Joplin, and Galena in Kansas. The town stands on high ground over solid limestone, near 950 feet above sea level.

Lead, zinc, and coal mines and quarries of Carthage “marble” lie in the neighbourhood, and the county court house is built of that stone. The city jobs goods for a fruit and grain region and makes lime, flour, furniture, bed springs, mining machinery, ploughs, and woollen goods. Factory products in 1905 were worth $1,179,661. Founded in 1833, Carthage became the county-seat in 1842. A Presbyterian collegiate institute, a yearly Chautauqua assembly, and a county fair complete the picture.
britannica-1911-casamari:
Casamari is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Cistercian abbey in the province of Rome, six miles east south east of Veroli. The abbey marks the site of Cereatae, the birthplace of Marius. Inscriptions show the place was later known as Cereatae Marianae. It stood as an independent community under the early empire, perhaps cut from the territory of Arpinum by the triumvirs.

The building itself is the entry's chief point. Casamari is a fine example of Burgundian early Gothic work, dated 1203 to 1217. In Italy only Fossanuova, built at almost the same time, stands beside it. The abbey survives very well preserved. A cited study by C. Enlart on the French origins of Gothic architecture in Italy points readers to the wider argument about how this style crossed the Alps.
britannica-1911-centumviri:
Centumviri, the hundred men, were an old court of civil law at Rome, said to have been set up by Servius Tullius. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica reads their age from their rites: the lance as sign of true ownership and the wager oath in claims for goods or freedom. Cicero places their field in the property counted at the census, so their word could make or unmake a citizen.

They also judged debts, and the common people had reason to guard the court from outside pressure. The members were never magistrates but judges, chosen for a fixed term, in Cicero's day by the tribal assembly. They numbered 105 then, and 180 by Pliny's time, their first count being unknown. The name also serves in inscriptions for town senates of a hundred members at Veii and Cures.
britannica-1911-chieri:
Chieri is a town and episcopal see of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Turin, 13 miles south-east of Turin by rail. Its people numbered 11,929 in the town and 13,803 in the commune in 1901. The Gothic cathedral, founded in 1037 and rebuilt in 1405, is the largest in Piedmont. A 13th century octagonal baptistery stands with it, and the town's past runs through bishops, counts and the house of Savoy.

Chieri was subject to the bishop of Turin in the 9th and 10th centuries, then became independent in the 11th century. In 1347 it submitted by choice to Count Amedeus VI of Savoy to escape the marquis of Monferrato. Savoy rule became final in the 16th century, and in 1785 the town was made a principality of the duke of Aosta. Trade and making came early, and by the mid 15th century it produced about 100,000 pieces of cotton goods a year.
britannica-1911-chillicothe-missouri:
Chillicothe is a city and the county-seat of Livingston county, Missouri, in the north of the state on the Grand river, about 80 miles north-east of Kansas City. Its people numbered 6,905 in 1900 and 6,265 in 1910, after 5,717 in 1890. Three railways serve the city, the Chicago, Milwaukee and St Paul, the Wabash and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy. Manufactures of various kinds are carried on there, the entry notes.

Coal and limestone are found in the vicinity, and much live stock is raised around the city. Wool and hides are shipped from Chillicothe as farm products of the district. Settlers came about 1830, and the town was laid out in 1837 on land granted directly by the Federal government. Incorporation followed in 1855. Rail links, minerals and stock raising together explain the town's place in its county.
britannica-1911-cori:
Cori is a town of the province of Rome in Italy. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on the lower slopes of the Volscian hills. It stands 1,300 feet above the sea, south east of Rome. Its people numbered 6,463 in 1901. The town holds the site of the old Volscian town of Cora. Old writers give its founding to Trojans, Volscians, or Latins. The Latin claim is held most likely.

Coins of Cora from before 250 before Christ still exist. Partisans of Marius wrecked the town in the civil wars. It had town rank before the republic fell. Then it fades from the record for long ages. Its walls draw the most ink in the entry. Three rings of wall enclose the upper town, lower town, and citadel. They are built in the rough Cyclopean style. A fine one arch bridge stands just outside the town.
britannica-1911-de-coster-charles-theodo:
Charles De Coster, the voice of Flanders, is drawn in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Munich in 1827, he was a Liége man's son. A Brussels bank desk held him till study called him back. In 1855 he finished his course at the university of Brussels. He helped found a small club of gay young letter men.

Verse in a new review was his first step into print. Rabelais and Montaigne were his close masters in prose style. Old French, he held, alone could catch Flemish speech and ways. His Flemish Legends of 1857 won praise, with art by friends. Ten years of work built his great prose epic of 1867. That tale of Thyl Uylenspiegel speaks Belgium's soul in arms.
britannica-1911-fatehpur-sikri:
Fatehpur Sikri is a town in the Agra district of the United Provinces of India, on the road from Agra to Jaipur, with 7,147 people in 1901. It is a ruined city of interest chiefly for its buildings. Akbar founded it in 1569 as a thank-offering for the birth of his son Selim, later the emperor Jahangir. The saint Selim Chisti had foretold that birth.

Its great mosque, said to be hardly surpassed in India, holds the white marble tomb of Selim Chisti, with pierced stone tracery. Other buildings include the palace of Jodh Bai, the five-storeyed Panch Mahal and Akbar's private apartments. The soft red sandstone could be carved almost like wood. Deserted within fifty years for lack of good water, the walled city keeps its carved fabric in ruin.
britannica-1911-giannutri:
Giannutri, an isle of Italy, is mapped in a short entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its Greek name ties it to a goddess of the hunt, and its Latin name says the same. It holds about one square mile in all. It lies south east of Giglio and south of a famed cape of the coast. Its top point stands three hundred and five feet above the sea.

The isle holds the ruins of a large Roman house of rest. That house stands near a bay on the east coast. Its parts fall in five groups in the text. A great tank in five parts heads the list. Rooms for the lords and for the slave hands come next, with store rooms and baths in the count. A view post rounds out the set.
britannica-1911-gori:
Gori is a town of Russian Transcaucasia in the government of Tiflis. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its schools, wine, and old fort. It stands on the river Kura northwest of Tiflis city. Its count in 1897 was about ten thousand people.

High land around the town makes a fine setting. A girls high school and a teacher school serve the district. Grain from Gori fields is reputed the best in Georgia. Its wine also holds a good name with buyers. Cool summer breezes keep the climate pleasant there. A Georgian king founded the town in 1123 for Armenian refugees. Persia wrecked its fort in the 1700s. East of town lies a rock cut town from the age of Alexander.
britannica-1911-gregoire-henri:
Henri Gregoire (1750-1831) was a French revolutionist and constitutional bishop of Blois, born at Veho near Luneville on 4 December 1750. The 1911 Britannica entry treats him as one of the Revolution's most principled churchmen. Note: his hosted file opens with the bibliography of the preceding article, on the Gregarines, before his own entry begins.

Gregoire's fame rests on his stand for the civil rights of Jews and of men of colour. It rests, too, on his work for the abolition of slavery in the French colonies. As bishop of Blois under the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, he held his see through the Revolution's storms. The entry follows his long public life, his scholarship, and his refusal to bend under later regimes. He stands in the volume as the priest who tried to wed the Church to the Revolution's best promises.
britannica-1911-guarnieri:
The Guarnieri were a celebrated family of violin-makers. They worked at Cremona. Andreas, the first, lived about 1626 to 1698. He worked beside Stradivari in Nicolo Amati's workshop. His son Joseph made instruments first like his father's. Later Joseph developed a style with a narrow waist. Another son, Peter of Cremona, settled at Mantua. A third, Peter of Venice, was also a fine maker.

The greatest of the family was Joseph del Gesù. He was Andreas' nephew and lived 1687 to 1745. His label bore the I.H.S. inscription, hence his title. Bold outline and massive build mark his work. He chased tone rather than visual perfection. His models vary greatly, showing constant experiment. Paganini's playing on a Joseph turned taste his way. Amateurs then favoured his robust tone over Amati sweetness. Many spurious instruments also flooded Europe after the middle of the 18th century.
britannica-1911-harith-ibn-hilliza-ul-ya: Harith ibn Hilliza ul Yashkuri was a pre Islamic Arabian poet of the tribe of Bakr in Arabia. His brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica states that nothing is known of the details of his life. He is famed solely as the author of one of the poems generally received among the Moallakat, the celebrated set of early Arabic odes. The notice gives no dates, no family facts, and no other works, and serves to place his name and tribe beside that famed poem.
britannica-1911-itri: Itri, in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, is a town of Campania in Italy, six miles by road north west of Formia. It stands in a scenic place in the mountains that the Via Appia crosses, with a population of 5,797 in 1901. Remains of the great wall that carried the ancient road survive in the town itself. The brigand Fra Diavolo was a native of Itri, which was once noted for brigandage.
britannica-1911-kansas-city-missouri:
Kansas City, Missouri, is a city of Jackson county, the second in size in the state. It stands where the Missouri and Kansas rivers meet, next to Kansas City, Kansas, and 235 miles west of St Louis. Its people numbered 132,716 in 1890, 163,752 in 1900, and 248,381 in 1910, among them many German, Irish, Swedish, and English born settlers.

Called the gateway to the Southwest, it is one of the great railway centres of the United States. A dozen lines serve it, among them the Union Pacific, the Missouri Pacific, the Santa Fé, and the Rock Island. Its rise in twenty years, from a river town to a quarter of a million people, is the spine of the piece.
britannica-1911-kashmiri:
Kashmiri, properly Kāśmīrī, is the name of the home language of the valley of Kashmir and the hills about it. Its segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kashmir article. In the census of 1901 its speakers were returned at 1,007,957. By origin it is the most southern member of the Dard group of the Piśāca languages.

Its kin are Shīnā, spoken round Gilgit, and Kōhistānī, spoken in the Indus hills. The wider family also counts Khōwār, the speech of Chitral, and the Kāfir group, of which Bashgali is the chief. Of all these tongues Kashmiri alone has a literature, or even an alphabet of its own. It is also the only one counted in the census of India, so no sure figures exist for the rest.
britannica-1911-kheri:
Kheri is a district of British India in the Lucknow division of the United Provinces, named for a small town with a railway station. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its size as 2,963 square miles and its people in 1901 as 905,138. Rivers cut the land into raised plateaus, each edged with rich low ground.

North of the Ul river the tract is an old lake bed, crossed by shifting streams and held to be very unhealthy. Stagnant water breeds lasting fevers there, yet folk live by the low ground since its soil is richer and cheaper to work. South of the Ul, flat plains hold marshes that swell into dangerous floods in the rains. Vast forests cover the north, about two-thirds of them sal trees, and a branch railway crosses the district.
britannica-1911-lacordaire-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Henri Lacordaire (1802–1861), French ecclesiastic and orator, was born at Recey-sur-Ource on the 12th of March 1802. He studied at Dijon, where his gift for rhetoric brought him local fame in the advocates' debates, and went on to practise law in Paris. Reading Lamennais's Essai sur l'Indifférence convinced his ardent nature, and in 1823 he entered the seminary of Saint-Sulpice. Ordained four years later, he became almoner of the college Henri IV.

He was called to help Lamennais edit L'Avenir. The journal argued that Catholicism belonged with liberty, equality and fraternity rather than with dynasty. Rome condemned the new teaching in an encyclical. Lacordaire later went to Rome, took the habit of a preaching friar at the Minerva, and wrote his Mémoire for restoring the Dominicans in France . Back in France in 1841 he resumed preaching at Notre Dame.
britannica-1911-lafont-pierre-cheri:
Pierre Chéri Lafont (1797–1873), French actor, was born at Bordeaux on the 15th of May 1797. He gave up work as an assistant ship's doctor in the navy and went to Paris to study singing and acting. The director of the Vaudeville engaged him, and he made his début there in 1821 in La Somnambule; his good looks and excellent voice soon made him a public favourite. After years at the Nouveautés and the Vaudeville, the burning of the latter in 1838 sent him to England, where he married Jenny Colon at Gretna Green and was soon divorced.

Back in Paris he joined the Variétés and acted there for fifteen years. Further engagements at the Vaudeville and the Gaiété followed. He ended his brilliant career at the Gymnase, playing the noble father. He died in Paris on the 19th of April 1873.
britannica-1911-larcher-pierre-henri:
Pierre Henri Larcher (1726-1812) was a French classical scholar and archaeologist, and his work is surveyed in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dijon, he was meant for the law but gave it up for the classics. A translation of a Greek romance in 1763 marked him as an excellent Greek scholar.

The entry notes his attack on Voltaire's history writing, which drew wide interest, and a study of Venus that won him a seat in the Academy of Inscriptions in 1778. His best work was a translation of Herodotus, published in 1786 after fifteen years of labor. The version itself is called dull but correct, while its rich commentary keeps its value.
britannica-1911-mallet-paul-henri:
Paul Henri Mallet (1730–1807) was a Swiss writer, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his turn to the north. He was born in Geneva on the twentieth of August 1730 and educated there. He then served as tutor in the family of the count of Calenberg in Saxony. In 1752 he became professor of belles lettres at Copenhagen.

At Copenhagen, Mallet was drawn to the old literature and history of his adopted land. In 1755 he published his Introduction to the history of Denmark. That work treated the religion, morals, laws, and customs of the ancient Danes. A second part dealt with the old literature of the country. It covered the mythology and poetry of the Celts, above all those of the north. His books opened the northern past to readers across Europe.
britannica-1911-malot-hector-henri:
Hector Henri Malot, a French writer of tales born in eighteen thirty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at La Bouille, the son of a notary, he studied law at Rouen and Paris. Letters drew his heart far more than law. He wrote for a great book of lives and for two journals.

He wrote a long run of tales of the life of his day. A set of three home tales heads the list in the text. More tales of kin, of a doctor, and of the law came year by year. Two of his books are held as fine tales for the young. One tells the road tale of a boy with no kin. A full set of his works came out late in his life.
britannica-1911-marri:
Marri is the name of a Baluch tribe on the border of Baluchistan, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its wars with the British. In the count of nineteen hundred and one the tribe held just past nineteen thousand souls. Its arms strength was put at about three thousand men. First ties with the British came in eighteen forty.

The tribe struck at the road links of an army that had passed the Bolan Pass. A bid to punish the tribe failed in a bad way. A force tried to storm a pass and was thrown back. Scores were slain and more died of heat and thirst. A fort the force meant to save was forced to yield with honors of war. In time the tribe joined the British against a foe tribe. New state craft then calmed the hills. The entry is a stark note on frontier war.
britannica-1911-martin-bon-louis-henri:
Bon Louis Henri Martin, a French historian who lived from 1810 to 1883, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at St Quentin, where his father was a judge. He trained as a notary and worked at that trade for a time. A tale of old times by him did well, and he turned to history.

With Paul Lacroix he planned a history of France built from the old chroniclers, with new matter to fill the gaps. The first volume came out in 1833 and led him to make the work his own. His History of France ran to fifteen volumes and was reworked in later editions. It won the first prize of the Academy in 1856 and a grand prize in 1869. The article grants the work faults: its Gauls owe more to romance than to fact.
britannica-1911-meilhac-henri:
Henri Meilhac, a French writer for the stage, gets a brief life note in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Paris in eighteen thirty one, he wrote light pieces for the press as a young man. Small stage farces in a brisk town style brought him to the front. Near eighteen sixty he met Ludovic Halevy and joined pens with him. That joint work for the stage ran for twenty years.

A few plays with lesser aides fill the rest of his list, the text says. The full tale of the joint work sits in the entry for Halevy, not here. In eighteen eighty eight he won a seat in the French Academy. He died at Paris in eighteen ninety seven. The note stays short and points the reader on for the works.
britannica-1911-melchers-julius-gari:
Julius Gari Melchers (born 1860) was an American artist, born at Detroit, Michigan, the son of a sculptor, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. At seventeen he was sent to Düsseldorf to study art, and after three years went to Paris to work at two art schools there. Drawn by the look of Holland, he settled at Egmond.

His first weighty Dutch picture, The Sermon, won honourable mention at the Paris Salon of 1886. He joined art bodies in New York, Berlin, Paris, London, and Munich, and won many medals and honours, among them the Legion of Honour of France. Besides portraits, his chief works named here include The Supper at Emmaus, The Family, and Mother and Child. He also painted the Peace and War decoration at the Congressional Library in Washington.
britannica-1911-ozieri:
Ozieri is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town of Sardinia. Ozieri lies in the province of Sassari, thirty-four miles from that city by rail. The town stands 1,280 feet above sea level on a steep slope. Because it faces north, the article judges it not very healthy. In the centre is a square with a fine fountain dated 1594.

The article notes the churches and the country round the town. The cathedral, restored in 1848, is the seat of the diocese of Bisarcio. The former cathedral stands to the north west and is a fine Romanesque building. The district is famous for its butter, the only butter made in Sardinia. Cattle are also bred there. The article closes with a reference to a history of Sardinian art for more on the old cathedral.
britannica-1911-pailleron-edouard-jules-:
Édouard Jules Henri Pailleron (1834-1899) was a French poet and dramatist, and this 1911 Britannica entry marks his high points. He was born in Paris and educated for the bar, but after pleading a single case he joined a dragoon regiment for two years. He travelled in northern Africa with an artist friend. Back in Paris in 1860 he brought out a volume of satires and a one-act play shown at the Odéon.

In 1862 he married the daughter of François Buloz, gaining a share in the Revue des deux mondes. His comedy Les Faux menages came in 1869. L'Étincelle, a bright one-act comedy of 1879, won another success. In 1881 Le Monde où l'on s'ennuie made one of the great hits of the age. That play mocked the academic society of the day, with open allusions to well-known people.
britannica-1911-ratnagiri:
Ratnagiri, a town and district of British India in the southern division of Bombay, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town stands on the seacoast south of Bombay, with about sixteen thousand people in 1901. A leading trade is the sardine fishery, which takes place in January and February and engages fleets of canoes.

The district forms a strip between the western Ghats and the sea, and its face is rugged. Near all its fertile land lies on stream banks. The coast runs about a hundred and fifty miles, rocky and dangerous near throughout. Rivers and bays open at intervals, each fit as a harbour for native craft, and the points at the river mouths are crowned with the ruins of old forts. The streams can be sailed for about twenty miles. At the start of British rule there were no roads at all.
britannica-1911-regnault-henri:
Henri Regnault, a French painter who lived from 1843 to 1871, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Paris, he was the son of Henri Victor Regnault. He passed through the studios of Montfort, Lamothe, and Cabanel. Beaten for the Grand Prix in 1863, he showed two plain portraits at the Salon the next year. In 1866 he won the Grand Prix with Thetis bringing the arms forged by Vulcan to Achilles.

Italy left him cold, but at Rome a school of rich colour took hold of him with growing force. In Spain he saw Prim at the head of his troops and painted that keen image. Judith, Salome, and a grim Moorish execution scene followed in quick order. When war came he fell in the front ranks at Buzenval on the 19th of January 1871, aged twenty-seven.
britannica-1911-rewari: Rewari, a town of British India in the Gurgaon district of the Punjab, is given a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood south west of Gurgaon on the Rajputana Malwa railway, with 27,295 people in 1901. The town was an important centre of trade, since it formed the junction for the Rewari Bhatinda branch of the Rajputana railway. Its chief manufacture was brass ware made for cooking utensils, so the brief piece joins a rail junction to a metal trade.
britannica-1911-rochefort-henri:
Henri Rochefort, marquis de Rochefort-Luçay, was a French politician born in Paris on 30 January 1830 and profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father was a noble who wrote light plays as Edmond Rochefort. His mother held republican views. Rochefort tried study as a doctor, clerk work, and play writing before he turned to the press.

He joined the Figaro staff in 1863. Sharp pieces that later formed a three volume set cost him that post. He then launched his own paper, La Lanterne. The state seized it, fined him 10000 francs, and gave him a year in prison. He kept it going from Brussels, and copies were smuggled into France in five tongues.
britannica-1911-ruwenzori:
Ruwenzori is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a high mountain range in central Africa, just north of the equator line. The range runs for about sixty five miles and holds peaks that rise above the snow line. Its west side falls in a steep drop to a deep rift valley.

The entry explains how the range was pushed up from the old rock floor of the land. It notes six groups of snowy peaks and heavy rain and cloud on the slopes. Streams fed by ice fields cut deep valleys on both sides. All of that water drains at last toward the Nile river system.
britannica-1911-sahyadri: Sahyadri, in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, is a mountain range of India. The term is Sanskrit rather than common speech. It is applied to the whole system of the Western Ghats, from the Tapti river to Cape Comorin. More narrowly, it names the part of that system in the Bombay Presidency, running south from Khandesh district toward Goa. A cross range in the Nizam's lands, forming the divide between two river systems, is also known by this name locally.
britannica-1911-saint-joseph-missouri:
Saint Joseph, a city in the north west corner of Missouri, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is the county seat of Buchanan County and a port of entry on the Missouri River. It ranks third in size among the cities of the state. Its count fell from 102,979 in 1900 to 77,403 in 1910.

Six railways serve Saint Joseph, and a steel bridge links it to Kansas. The city is laid out on hills above the river bluffs. Its chief buildings list a court house, a hall that seats seven thousand, and a public library. Six parks serve the town. Great stock yards in South Saint Joseph draw much note. A board form of rule began in 1910.
britannica-1911-sutri:
Sutri is a town and bishop see of Italy in the province of Rome, set out in a 1911 Britannica entry. It stands on a narrow hill ringed by ravines at nine hundred and fifty five feet. A slim neck of land on the west alone joins it to the country round. The town held about two thousand seven hundred people at its count.

Old walls of tufa blocks and rock cut sewers mark its ancient Sutrium past. The cathedral is modern, yet its crypt with twenty columns is old work. A bell tower of the 1200s rises by that church in the town. Rock cut church and Roman amphitheatre hewn in cliffs face it across the gorge.
britannica-1911-tauri:
Tauri were the first known folk of the mountain coast of the south Crimea, as an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells. Herodotus speaks of them. Nothing sure is known of their kin. They may be an old stock tied to some race of the Caucasus, and they are not likely to be Celts, for all the likeness of their name to Taurisci.

They were famed in the old world for their maiden goddess, whom the Greeks matched with Artemis or with Iphigeneia. The goddess was said to have been brought to her shrine at the hour she was to be slain at Aulis. Their grim custom was to offer shipwrecked strangers to her, the root of the tale of Orestes and his sister. Plays by Euripides and by Goethe take up that tale. Late in the second century before Christ the Tauri served the Scythian king Scilurus.
britannica-1911-tresviri:
Tresviri is the subject of a Roman entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word names a board of three men in Rome. Such boards held set posts or were picked for a task. The first kind named dealt with crime and courts. They were first set up about 289 before Christ. They had no power of arrest in their own right. They acted as agents for higher officers of state.

They kept watch over prisoners in their charge. They carried out death rulings passed by the courts. They took in the accused and kept streets in order. Night rounds and fire calls fell to them as well. They helped burn banned books at need for the state. Sums left as pledges in suits were kept by them. Caesar raised their count to four for a time. Augustus brought the count back to three in his reign.
britannica-1911-turbet-i-haidari:
Turbet i Haidari is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a district in the province of Khorasan, in Persia. It is bounded by Meshed, Bakharz, Khaf, and Turshiz. Its people number about thirty thousand. Most of them are of the Turki Karai tribe, settled there by Timur in the fourteenth century, and Beluchis.

The Karais supply a battalion of foot soldiers and one hundred and fifty horsemen to the army. The district holds about one hundred and fifty villages, most of them in its richer eastern part. It pays a yearly revenue of fourteen thousand pounds. Much silk was once made there, but now very little, though grain crops are large. The chief town, of the same name, stands seventy-six miles south of Meshed at a height of 4,100 feet.
britannica-1911-velletri:
Velletri, a town in the province of Rome, Italy, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In ancient times it was called Velitrae. It stands at the south east foot of the outer wall of the Alban crater. Rome lies twenty six miles north west by rail, and the town sits 1,155 feet above the sea.

The entry gives it 14,243 people in the town and 18,734 in the commune in 1901. Good wine is made from the rich vineyards around it, and a state test station for wine growing stands there. The town looks out over the Volscian mountains and the Pomptine Marshes. Sights named include the town palace with old inscriptions and the Palazzo Ginetti with its odd detached staircase. The tall bell tower of a church was raised in 1353, in thanks for the end of a plague.
cap-n-eri:
Joseph Crosby Lincoln set this novel in a Cape Cod village, where Captain Eri Hazeltine keeps house with two other retired sea captains, all bachelors and all set in their ways. The contents promise the trouble early: a lamb for the sacrifice, the train coming in, and, fifth, the woman from Nantucket. The captains' household cannot run itself, and the village watches them try.

A housekeeper is engaged, and Mrs. Snow's arrival from Nantucket reorders the house and its three old salts. Lincoln builds comedy from shipboard habits carried ashore: watches kept, orders given, and a cable tested like a ship's line. Eri, the lamb of the first chapter, finds himself the one marked out by fate and by the schoolhouse bell. It is a courtship novel in oilskins, and it made Lincoln's name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostini-agaz:
Agostini Agazzari, musical composer of Siena's noble families, was born 2 December 1578. He died probably 10 April 1640; his first working years served Emperor Matthias. Rome took him about 1600 to succeed Anerio as the German College's maestro di cappella. Later he served at St. Apollinaris and the Roman Seminary. His final musical education came from Viadana of Mantua.

Both men share credit for developing thoroughbass and teaching the correct method of figuring a bass. In 1630 he returned to Siena, becoming maestro of the cathedral, and died holding that post. He belonged to the Academy of Armonici Intronati and ranked among the Roman school's most fruitful composers. His many works include masses from 1596 to 1608, motets, Magnificats, and litanies, often republished and praised in Proske's Musica divina. He also wrote the drama Eumelio for a wedding in 1614.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alatri:
Alatri is an Italian bishopric under the Holy See's immediate jurisdiction, comprising seven towns in Rome province. Its closeness to Rome argues Christianity was taught there very early. This does not compel belief in local legends placing the conversion of Ferentino, Alatri, and neighbouring towns in the apostolic age. The route of Italy's earliest Gospel preachers remains unknown. The first bishop of Alatri met in history is Paschasius in 551, who accompanied Pope Vigilius to Constantinople during the Three Chapters controversy.

In Alatri's church of St. Mary Major is preserved a wooden Madonna statue, a splendid example of twelfth-century Roman art. Alatri counts 16 parishes and 77 churches, chapels, and oratories. It has 64 secular priests and 52 seminarians, with 42 regular clergy, 31 lay brothers, and 81 women religious. There are 30 confraternities, one boys' school with 87 pupils, and three girls' schools with 30 pupils. Its population is 24,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-se:
Alessandro Serpieri was an Italian priest, astronomer, and seismologist, born near Rimini in October 1823 and dead at Fiesole in February 1885. Educated by the Piarist fathers at Urbino, he entered their novitiate at Florence in 1838 and studied philosophy and the sciences at the Ximenian College and observatory. In 1846 he became professor of philosophy and physics at Urbino, and in 1848 he was ordained a priest, later rector of the college.

Serpieri's merit as an astronomer lay in watching shooting stars. His first treatise dates from 1847, and in August 1850 he found that the August meteors stream from a point near Gamma Persei, giving the Perseids their name. His greatest work was in seismology. His study of the earthquake of 12 March 1873 was called a model of scientific analysis by de Rossi, and it first used the idea of a seismic radiant. His masterwork treated the earthquake of March 1875 with 240 documents from a hundred places.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allori:
The Allori were Florentine painters spanning three generations. Angiolo di Cosimo, called Il Bronzino, was an able painter and poet, born at Monticello near Florence in 1502 and dead at Florence in 1572. A pupil of Raffaelino del Garbo and later of Jacopo da Pontormo, he assisted Pontormo and completed his unfinished works. He became court painter to Cosimo I, Grand Duke of Tuscany. Among his portraits are those of Dante and Petrarch.

His nephew Alessandro Allori, born at Florence in 1535 and dead there in 1607, was an able artist patronized by Grand Duke Francesco. Alessandro's son Cristofano Allori, known as Bronzino the Younger, was born at Florence in 1577 and dead there in 1621. A pupil of his father, of Santo di Tito, and of Cigoli, and of somewhat irregular life, he was a painter of talent in both figure and landscape. He ranked among the Florentine school's best colourists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselmo-bandu:
Anselmo Banduri, archaeologist and coin scholar, born 1671, died 1743. He joined the Benedictines young and studied at Naples, then Florence. Here he met Montfaucon, seeking Chrysostom manuscripts in Italy. Banduri served him well and was recommended to Cosimo III for a Pavia chair. It was suggested he be sent to Paris for preparation. After a short stay at Rome, Banduri went to Paris.

In 1711 he published at Paris his Imperium Orientale, an illustrated Byzantine work from medieval Greek manuscripts, some then first made known. He defended himself against Casimir Oudin, attacking from second-hand knowledge. In 1718 he published at Paris two volumes on coinage from Trajan to the last Palaeologi. Of this work Father Eckhel says it contains few important contributions. The bibliography he prefixed to it was reprinted by Fabricius at Hamburg in 1719. In 1715 he became an honorary member of the Academy of Inscriptions, and in 1724 Orléans librarian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antivari:
Antivari, an old Adriatic port facing Bari across the sea, served as the Catholic archbishop's seat in Montenegro. Its bishops claimed roots in the fifth century, with a firm see by the ninth and a refounding in the twelfth. Over the centuries the town passed from Greek emperors to a small Dalmatian republic, then to Serb kings, Hungary, and Venice.

Venetian rule brought nearly a century of peace and busy trade, until Ottoman forces besieged the town in 1538. Later treaties handed it to Montenegro, and in 1886 its archdiocese came directly under the Holy See. A decree of 1902 restored its old rank as primatial see of Dalmatia, closing the story of a small port caught between empires, faiths, and shifting borders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-alleg:
Antonio Allegri, called Correggio after his Lombard birthplace, was born in 1494 and died in 1534. A merchant's son, he left no writings, had no known teachers or pupils, and never courted great patrons. From 1518 to 1530 he worked chiefly at Parma, then returned to his native town for his final years.

His genius unfolded away from art centres, in tender Madonnas, myth scenes such as Danae, and the Madonna del Latte. Vasari, writing in 1542, found no portrait or sketch of him in Lombardy, so little trace had he left. The entry presents a quiet master whose soft light and grace made him, in its words, the Master of Parma.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-neri:
Florentine priest and chemist Antonio Neri, who died in 1614 after a life of which few details survive, wrote the book that long ruled the craft of glassmaking. He travelled in Italy and Holland gathering knowledge of how glass was made, coloured, and used to imitate precious stones. He published it as L'Arte Vetraria, the Art of Glassmaking, at Florence in 1612. For a long time most later works on the subject rested on it.

The original appeared in three editions, Florence 1612 and 1661 and Milan 1817. An English physician, Dr. Merret, turned it into Latin in 1662 with notes of his own, and Johann Kunckel published a revised German edition in 1689. A French version followed about a century later. The entry is frank about gaps in Neri's biography, yet clear on why his manual mattered to makers for generations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-strad:
Cremonese violin maker Antonio Stradivari, born in 1649 or 1650 and dead at Cremona in December 1737, built the instruments that still set the standard for string sound. No parish record of his birth survives at Cremona, so he was probably born in a nearby village. He began making stringed instruments in 1667, likely as a pupil in the workshop of Nicholas Amati, whose signed violins of that date may hide Stradivari's early hand.

In 1680 he set up on his own in the Piazza San Domenico and soon won fame. He improved Amati's model with better arching, more exact wood thickness, a changed scroll, and richer varnish. His finest instruments date from 1698 to 1725, when design, choice of wood, and finish reached their height. The entry follows a craftsman from workshop pupil to master whose name became shorthand for a perfect violin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bari:
Bari is an archdiocese in Apulia, southern Italy, its city the province's chief town on an Adriatic peninsula. Ancient Barium fell to Rome after the war with Pyrrhus yet kept its autonomy. As a seaport facing the East, it likely received Christianity very early, and tradition says St Peter preached there. Its first known bishop, Gervasius, attended Sardica in 347, and later bishops appear at Constantinople's orbit and Nicaea in 780.

Saracens wasted Apulia in the ninth century and seized Bari, but Byzantium retook it in 841. In 844 Angelarius of ruined Canosa brought relics of Rufinus, Memorus, and Sabinus to Bari, winning the double title Bari and Canosa. John XI granted the pallium in 933, and Giovanni II broke from Constantinople in 952. The diocese later counted 300,400 people, 33 parishes, 260 churches and chapels, and 250 secular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonaventura-c:
Bonaventura Cavalieri, an Italian mathematician and disciple of Galileo, gave geometry his Method of Indivisibles, a forerunner of integral calculus. Born at Milan in 1598, he joined the Jesuates at fifteen and studied under Castelli at Pisa. In 1629 he took the mathematics chair at Bologna, teaching there until his death in 1647 despite years of gout.

His Geometria of 1635 treats lines as endless points, surfaces as endless lines, and solids as endless surfaces, improving on the older Greek method. Pain from gout dogged him for years, and he turned to mathematics for relief, as Pascal had done. Guldinus attacked the idea as unsound, and Cavalieri answered in his Exercitationes Geometricae of 1647, which also first proved Pappus's theorem in full. He also spread the use of logarithms in Italy and wrote on conic sections, planets, and trigonometry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonizo-of-sut:
Bonizo of Sutri, an eleventh-century bishop and Gregorian partisan, chronicled his own age of pope against emperor. Born about 1045, probably at Cremona, he joined the Pataria reform party and clashed as subdeacon with the bishop of Piacenza. Gregory VII made him Bishop of Sutri in 1074, and he served as papal legate at Cremona in 1078.

Seized by Henry IV in 1082 and held by the antipope Clement III, he escaped after a year and sheltered with Countess Matilda of Tuscany. Elected to Piacenza in 1086, he took possession only in 1088 with Urban II's backing, and his enemies had him killed on 14 July 1090. His writings include the Decretum on church law and morals and the Liber ad amicum, a Church history from his own time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cagliari:
Cagliari, ancient Caralis, is the chief city and capital of Sardinia and a port on the Gulf of Cagliari. Carthaginians founded it, and Romans took it after the War of the Mercenaries. Vandals seized it in the fifth century, and Saracens held it in the eighth until Pisans helped expel them in 1022. Aragon took the city in 1324, and it stayed Spanish until 1714, passing in 1717 to the Duke of Savoy.

Its best known early bishop is Lucifer. From 354 to 371 he championed orthodoxy against Arianism as a friend of Saint Athanasius, yet late in life he authored a schism that bears his name. Under the Vandals, Sardinia sheltered Catholic bishops fleeing North Africa, among them Saints Eugenius and Fulgentius. Earlier bishops include Quintasius, present at Arles in 314, and Thomas and Januarius, named in Saint Gregory the Great's letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carbonari:
The Carbonari, or charcoal-burners, were a secret political society active chiefly in France and Italy in the early nineteenth century. Born from the political ferment of the French Revolution, the society first showed its power in Naples and the Papal States. Claims of an older origin, with Francis I of France as protector, are dismissed by the entry as improbable.

Members borrowed the charcoal trade's language for their secret life. The meeting place was a hut, its inner room a coal shop, and its surroundings a forest. Members called each other good cousin and outsiders heathens. Divided into apprentices and a higher grade, the society later declined, lingered briefly as a democratic Charbonnerie among French republicans until after 1841, and counted fewer members in Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathari:
Cathari, from the Greek word for pure, was a name given to several sects at different periods. Third-century Novatians and Manichaeans bore it, but it most often denotes the dualist sects of the later Middle Ages. They went by many other names as well. Some came from their trades, some from their leaders, and some from the towns where they gathered, including Albigenses from Albi.

The article sets out their dualist principles and then follows their history country by country: Italy, Germany and England, and the Balkan states. It closes by describing their relations with the Catholic Church. That account covers the preaching and inquisitorial campaigns mounted against them, and points readers to the sources for each region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chiavari:
On the Ligurian coast of northern Italy, the Diocese of Chiavari serves a city famed for fishing, slate, and cherrywood chairs.
